reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
In this study, Wang et al. reported the impact of Chitinase-like protein 3 (Chil3) and its human functional homolog chitinase-
3-like 2 (CHI3L2) on macrophage lipid metabolism and atherosclerosis. Using numerous elegant experimental approaches
as well as in in vitro and in vivo models, the authors proposed a new autocrine mechanism in which secreted CLP regulates
cholesterol uptake in macrophages through binding to CD36. Importantly, Wang et al. provided important new therapeutic
insights with the use of antibodies targeting CHI3L2 which attenuate atherosclerosis. This group previously demonstrated
that Chil3 polymorphisms were associated with inflammatory diseases by regulating lipid metabolism. This study is in the
continuation of their previous works by positioning Chil3 in the development of atherosclerosis. The overall study is very
interesting but several points must be clarified by the authors.
Major points.
1. Previous numerous studies characterized several macrophage populations in atherosclerotic plaques by single-cell RNA-
Sequencing (PMID: 38639096, PMID: 29545366, PMID: 31591603, PMID: 32981416….). Was Chil3 expression associated
with a specific subtype cluster of macrophages in atherosclerotic plaques (Trem2+ macrophages (PMID: 38646596)) ? Was
this latter altered upon Chil3 deficiency ? Analysis of Chil3 expression in CAM (classically activated macrophages) and
AAM (alternatively activated macrophages) is indeed very limited (Extended Data Fig. 2e-h).
2. Because lipid uptake in macrophages has a profound impact on intracellular lipid homeostasis beyond foam cell
formation, it is important to further describe the consequences of the alteration of Chil3 expression in the lipidome of
macrophages, especially in membrane lipid composition. Then, lipidome of WT and Chil3  macrophages must be explored
in order to decipher the role of Chil3 in macrophages. Such an analysis is even more essential since Chil3 deficiency allows
an increased expression of Abcg1, a transporter recently identified as playing a key role in lipid rewiring and functions of
macrophages (beyond cholesterol efflux) (PMID: 39661702).
3. Through the uptake of oxidized lipids and free fatty acids, CD36 plays major roles in several pathways controlling the
metabolic phenotype of macrophage (fatty acid oxidation and storage, ROS production, energy metabolism….). The authors
must provide information about the impact of Chil3 deficiency on metabolic pathways in macrophages (RNA-sequencing
and/or seahorse analyses for example).
4. The authors did not explain and discuss the role of Chil3 on inflammation, especially on the inflammatory phenotype of
macrophages. Because CD36, the main target of Chil3, is involved in NLRP3 activation (PMID: 23812099), the reduced IL-
1β expression observed in aorta of Chil3  mice (Fig1e) could result from an impaired activation of the NLRP3 pathway.
Although the role of Chil3 in foam cell formation is very likely involved in the attenuated atherosclerosis development, the
authors cannot exclude the role of inflammation in their mechanism since antiiflammatory targeting IL-1β led to a reduction of
atherosclerotic cardiovascular diseases (PMID: 28845751). The authors must explore and/or discuss this aspect.
Others major points.
5. In mice with a total Chil3 deficiency, what tissue drives the circulating Chil3 / CHI3L2 concentrations in mice (Fig. 1a, 
Extended data Fig. 2i……) ? Same question in humans (Fig. 2c)?
6. Extended Data Fig. 1(a). What was the diet of ApoE-/- and WT mice ?
7. Fig. 1c. The title of the Y-axis must be clarified. What class of lipid was
quantified ? Cholesterol ? How was quantified the
lipid profile? How do the authors explain the reduced serum LDL (likely LDL-C) in BQ.ApoE-/-.Chil3-/- mice in comparison to
BQ.ApoE-/- mice ? Same comments in Fig. 2e).
8. Same question with oxLDL (Fig. 1d).
9. Fig. 2k. The efficiency of the treatment with rhCHI3L2 must be validated by quantification of CHI3L2 in the circulation of
mice following intraperitoneal injection.
10. Figure 3. Single-cell RNA-Sequencing data are interesting but it would be
useful to know the biological pathways that
are altered in macrophages in the three mouse models (WT, Chi  and Chil3 .CHI3L2tg). A same comment can be done in
BMDM and PM cells (Figure 5). As a whole, impact of Chil3 deletion as well as expression of CHI3L2 in Chil3-deficient cells
on the metabolic phenotype of macrophages is lacking. In this context, it is very intriguing that no cholesterol metabolism (or
lipid metabolism) pathways were found altered by RNA-sequencing in oxLDL stimulated Chil3  versus WT BMDM
(Extended Data Fig. 7b). These findings weaken a significant role of Chil3 in macrophage lipid uptake as proposed by the
authors.
11. Figure 6. Although not in the top 5 candidate, were P2Y6R and TREM2 (or some TLRs) identified in IP and MS analyses
since these receptors promote lipid uptake and atherosclerosis (PMID: 38036416, PMID: 38646596) ?
12. As a follow up of my previous comment, may Chil3 promote hydrolysis of N-glycosylated glycans of others membrane
proteins without physically interacting with them (and then not to be detected by co-IP) ?
13. Figure 8a. How do the authors explain that the impaired cholesterol uptake in Chil3  BMDM was not accompanied by an
increased expression of Ldlr and Hmgcoar genes; the expression of these genes being downregulated by cholesterol.
14. Figure 8d. Although the method used to quantify cholesterol efflux is highly questionable, the results are quite intriguing.
Indeed, a 45% cholesterol efflux during a 4h incubation with HDL is extremely high (about 10% is expected) and suggests
an alteration of cell viability. The authors must describe the method used (what type of HDL used ? what is the % of
cholesterol efflux without HDL ? ……..).
15. Extended Data Fig. 7d and Figure 8. The authors proposed that the increased Abcg1 expression resulted from an
elevation of Ppar  expression. If it is the case, Abca1 expression would be also increased since induction of Ppar  stimulates
Abca1 expression (PMID: 11135616)
16. Figures 8e-g. It is difficult to conclude on these experiments in the absence of the WT BMDM. More importantly, the
authors proposed that the reduced cholesterol uptake (in the presence of oxLDL) in Chil3  BMDM increases Abcg1
expression through alteration of mTOR and induction of Ppar  expression. Such a mechanism is not coherent with the fact
that oxysterols are potent activators of Abcg1 expression through the LXR pathway (PMID: 16024918). Indeed, Abcg1
expression is increased when macrophages are incubated with oxLDL (source of oxysterols) as confirmed in Fig. 8e-f. Then,
it would be expected to observe a reduced Abcg1 expression in Chil3  BMDM as a consequence of the impaired oxLDL
uptake. How do the authors reconcile these potential conflicting observations ?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This study focuses on the role of chitinase-like proteins in atherosclerosis.
Major:
1) General: how is LDL-cholesterol measured? This usually does not accumulate at high levels in the plasma of ApoE-/- 
mice. The authors need to be far more thorough here, especially since they state that they find differences.
2) The authors several times refer to WT mice. It is well known that WT mice do not develop atherosclerosis, so it does not
make sense that atherosclerosis would be studied in this particular model. The authors need to clarify this for each and
every study. Fig 2k-m. Were these wild-type mice? Or Ldlr-/- mice? This needs to be clarified in the text. Line 207. Again, I
am confused as to the mouse models here. WT mice do not develop atherosclerosis. The authors need to really clarify this
better. Fig 4c-g. What was the genotype of the recipients of the mice for bone marrow transplantation? Please clarify. It is
impossible that these were just CD45.2 mice without any mutation since these mice do not develop atherosclerosis.
3) The number of mice for any analysis in atherosclerosis experiments needs to be at least n=10. In very many figures, these
numbers are lower; real conclusions can therefore not be drawn.
4) The authors need to provide more definitive evidence, preferably in vivo, that the upregulation of CD36 is what accounts for their phenotype. Was CD36 staining increased in atherosclerotic plaques?
5) Extended Data Fig 1a. These data on Chil3 being upregulated are not that convincing. I understand the use of public
datasets, which in general makes things easier, but it seems to me that the n would need to be increased to really conclude
that Chil1 and Chid1 are not affected. These experiments are not hard to do and would need to be performed in order for the
authors to really draw conclusions here.
6) Fig 2c. How has plasma from ‘control’ and ‘atherosclerosis’ been defined? This would require a far more extensive
description. Also here the x-axis crosses the y-axis at 3.0, with the intention to magnify a small, though significant, increase.
What is the extent of the increase shown in Fig 2c? Why were the data log-transformed?
7) Fig 2f. Again, the x-axis is not crossing 0. Why making so much of the small difference in oxLDL? What is the extent of the
increase? And what is the extent of the increase in LDL in Fig 2e?
8) Fig 2i-j. Too few datapoints have been included. The data in Fig 2g-h suggest more mice were included in these studies;
the same number would need to be included in Fig 2i-j.
9) Fig 1a. This is a very strange way to display the data with the x-axis crossing the y-axis at -200. This would need to be
changed to 0. If there are values lower than 0 they would need to be adjusted to 0.
10) Extended Fig 2d. What do the authors mean with a proliferative cell?
11) Extended Fig 2i. This is a minimal difference. The x-axis should not cross at 4.0, but at 0.0; otherwise the authors make
too much of a maybe not even 5% difference, which I do not view as meaningful.
12) Extended Fig 2f and 2h. The number of replicates should at least be increased to n=4. Preferably n=6. N=3 is
insufficient. Data on THP-1 cells would need to be complemented by data on PBMCs differentiated in what the authors refer
to as AAMs or CAMs; THP-1 cells are already very activated since they are differentiated into macrophages employing PMA.
13) Fig 4a. More examples on co-localization would need to be shown. The examples in Fig 4b on co-localization are too
unclear to draw conclusions.
14) Fig 4b. What is meant by APS and FPS? Again, there is an unclarity here. This makes it hard to read and properly
review this manuscript.
15) Fig 4h. The chlodronate experiment is usually performed as a way to study monocyte infiltration into atherosclerotic
plaques. The transferred monocytes are labeled with beads, so that homing of monocytes to plaques can be studied. Such
an experiment is actually never performed with bone marrow derived macrophages. If performed in this way, macrophages
need to be labeled so their fate can be studied better. It is unclear what the authors have done in Fig 4h-k. It seems rather to
me that they have performed a bone marrow transplantation without performing the irradiation first. If the authors claim that
the phenotype is macrophage-driven, they will need to create a macrophage-specific knockout. That is only the proper way
that is widely accepted in the field.
16) Extended Figure 4f. The flow cytometry plots are insufficient in showing that the transfer with macrophages actually led to
accumulation of considerable amount of macrophages in the aorta. The method needs to be established first.
17) Extended Fig 5a-c. These calculated interactions actually do not tell us that much. What is exactly happening here and
what is the biological nature of these interactions.
18) Extended Fig 5d. If the authors really want to draw a conclusion on macrophages, they need to perform laser capture
microscopy on atherosclerotic plaques, or single cell RNASeq, but they cannot do this by performing whole RNA extraction
on the aorta.
19) Extended Fig 5e. When were these macrophages isolated? It is impossible to directly isolate BMDMs; then these cells
would be bone marrow monocytes. This would need to be clarified. How was the experiment performed?
20) Extended Fig 5f-j. Same questions – how were these experiments performed? This needs to be stated in the figure
legends or better described in the main text. If the authors claim more oxLDL uptake, ideally they perform mass-spec on their
macrophages to show that free cholesterol and cholesteryl esters are increased. This is the only definitive measure. These
mfi measurements tell us very little, and again, in extended Fig 5j, differences are minor for BMDMs. I do not understand the
significant p-values. The authors are making too much of these data.
21) Fig 6i-k. Were these intracellular stainings? Ideally the authors would complement these data with mass spec
measurements of free cholesterol and cholesteryl esters.
22) Text line 474. The authors imply that Mylip would be involved in the cholesterol efflux pathway while it in fact induces the
degradation of the Ldl receptor.
23) Fig 8. It is of interest that mainly Abcg1 is affected in Chil-3 deficiency. How do the authors explain that this particular
transporter is affected and not Abca1? What would the mechanism be underlying this finding?
24) Related to this, Abcg1 deficiency does not affect atherosclerotic lesion area or decreases it. This does not align with the
findings of the authors. Please explain.
25) How would lipid deposition activate mTOR?
26) Line 557 – the authors are discussing ‘inflammatory foamy macrophages’. But the foamy macrophages are generally
considered to be anti-inflammatory.
Minor:
1) Keywords: atherosclerogenesis (also in lines 101 and 110). This is not a usual word. It is atherosclerosis or
atherogenesis.
2) Introduction: line 82 – it probably needs to state: various transformations, such as those into…
3) Also in lines 83-84 it is implied that the switch to other phenotypes accounts for SMCs taking up lipid. This is simply not
true. Lipid uptake by SMCs accounts fort heir differentiation into macrophages for example. Please adjust the text
accordingly.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Answer: We thank you for raising this important point. Our initial focus on male
mic in studies of chitinase-like proteins (CLPs, mainly Chil3 and CHI3L2) was
based on methodological and conceptual considerations, not an assumption of
sex-specific effects. Additional experiments showed that Chil3-deficient mice
are resistant to atherosclerosis in both sexes. While female mice generally
exhibit a more protective response due to hormones (e.g., estrogen)1, we also
evaluated female mice in a 3-month Western diet (WD) model across three
genetically modified strains (ApoE-/-, ApoE-/-.Chil3∆ and ApoE-/-.Chil3∆.CHI3L2tg
mice) and observed effects comparable to males, despite smaller plaque areas
(Fig. 1 in this letter). These findings suggest that CLPs exert no major sex-
specific effect on atherosclerosis. The new results have been included in the
revised manuscript as Fig. 2.
Our core hypothesis posits that Chil3 deficiency exerts its anti-atherosclerotic
effects through intrinsic macrophage mechanisms. To test this, we conducted
in vitro studies using macrophages from male and female mice. For early
analyses such as lipid accumulation, primary macrophages were isolated
separately from male and female mice within the same batch, and the effect of
Chil3 on lipid deposition was assessed. Consistent results were observed
across both sexes (Fig. 2 in this letter, also in the revised manuscript as
Extended Data Fig. 5a), strongly indicating that the core cellular function
of Chil3 is not sex-dependent. Therefore, the mechanisms described are
likely applicable to both male and female mice. Subsequent experiments used
the same batch of cells and aimed for balanced male-to-female ratios across
genotypes, with the sex of each macrophage source indicated in the figure
legend.
Fig. 1. CLPs promote the formation of atherosclerosis.
Fig. 2. Chil3 promotes lipid deposition in macrophages.
2. The CD68 staining in Fig. 1h appears non-specific, as the green fluorescence
shows strong background signal, making it difficult to assess true CD68
expression. Since CD68 is a macrophage marker expressed in atherosclerotic
lesions, it is important to clearly demonstrate specific staining. Additionally, co-
staining CD68 with α-SMA could better illustrate the stability of the plaques
within the lesion instead of IHC staining of α-SMA. In Fig. 1i, the lesion
boundaries are not clearly defined—adding an outline would improve clarity. It
is also unclear whether the selected image accurately represents reduced
lesion size in Chil3-deficient mice. How is the expression of ICAM1 and VCAM-
1 levels in the lesions? The above comment is applicable to the other Figures
(2i, j…)
Answer: Thanks. We have performed additional experiments and image
analyses to address each point raised, as detailed below.
Point 1: CD68/α-SMA co-staining
Response: We conducted new double immunofluorescence staining for CD68
and α-SMA on aortic root sections from ApoE-/-, ApoE-/-.Chil3∆ and ApoE-
/-.Chil3∆.hCHI3L2tg littermate mice (Fig. 1f-g in this letter). The co-staining
clearly shows the distribution of macrophage (CD68+) and α-SMA, supporting
our conclusion that CLP deficiency promotes a more stable plaque phenotype
with reduced macrophage content.
Point 2: Lesion boundaries and representation of lesion size reduction
Response: Lesion boundaries in representative images were delineated with
white or black dashed lines for clarity (For representative images, please refer
to Fig. 1, 3 in this letter). For further details, please refer to the revised
manuscript, which includes all animal experimental results. Additionally, we
have examined the selected representative images to ensure they accurately
reflect the severity of lesions in each genetically modified mouse.
Point 3: ICAM-1 and VCAM-1 expression

increase in VCAM-1, but not ICAM-1, in lesions of ApoE-/- and ApoE-
/-.Chil3∆.hCHI3L2tg mice compared to ApoE-/-.Chil3∆ mice (Fig. 1f-g in this
letter). These findings indicate that CLPs preferentially regulate VCAM-1-
associated leukocyte recruitment pathways, without broadly affecting ICAM-1-
mediated endothelial activation.
3. The authors used a collection time of 5 months after Western diet feeding.
Did earlier time points fail to show the changes observed at 5 months?
If so,
what does this say about the role of CLPs in atherosclerosis initiation? At the
same time, the treatment regimen described in Fig. 9c started at 3 months,
which only accounts for the prevention of plaque progression. While interesting,
the most clinically important model would assess plaque regression following

Answer: We apologize for the confusion caused by our original schematic
diagram. The atherosclerosis model consistently used a 3-month induction
period: 2-month-old mice were fed a WD for 3 months, reaching 5 months of
age at the endpoint. We have recognized that the schematic diagram is
misleading and somewhat redundant in presenting the genotype-phenotype
relationship. Therefore, we have removed this diagram while ensuring that the
 that the
modeling period remains 3 months. However, the schematic diagram for the
neutralizing antibody efficacy experiment has been corrected (Fig. 3c in this
letter).
In this study, all models used a 3-month WD, a standard early- to mid-stage
atherosclerosis model in many classic studies2,3, facilitating data comparison.
Within 3 months, lipid deposition, inflammatory responses, macrophage
activation, and cholesterol metabolism changes are evident, providing a
convenient window to assess interventions. WD beyond 3 months leads to
more mature plaques with calcification, modeling late-stage lesions. Thus, we
focused here on CLP effects in early- to mid-stage atherosclerosis, while our
recent work addresses late-stage disease, including VSMC calcification.
For evaluating the CHI3L2 neutralizing antibody, treatment was initiated in 2-
month-old mice after 1 month of WD feeding to induce CHI3L2 expression,
based on our previous findings that circulating CLPs are elevated in
atherosclerotic serum and in ox-LDL-stimulated macrophage-derived foam
cells. Mice continued with WD for additional 2 months, with the antibody
administered via tail vein injection at the start of the second and third months.
This model was primarily designed to assess the preventive effect of the
antibody (Fig. 3c-e in this letter).
Following your suggestion, we also tested the therapeutic potential of the
CHI3L2 antibody to promote plaque regression, which is clinically relevant.
ApoE-/-.Chil3∆.hCHI3L2tg mice were fed WD for 3 months to establish plaques,
then randomized to ND for 1 month with either isotype IgG or CHI3L2
neutralizing antibody (Fig. 3f). CHI3L2 antibody treatment markedly enhanced
plaque regression and reduced lesion volume compared to diet switching alone
(Fig. 3g-h in this letter).
These findings support our central hypothesis and enhance the clinical
translational value of our work. The results indicate that targeting CHI3L2
not only prevents disease progression but, in combination with dietary
intervention, can actively reverse pre-existing lesions. The new results
have been included in the revised manuscript as Fig. 9.
Fig. 3. Targeting CHI3L2 could block the progression of atherosclerosis.

and CHI3L2 transgenic mice, but not in Chil3-/- mice. These findings might be

Answer: Thanks. We performed co-culture experiments. Primary bone
marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs) were isolated from ApoE-/-, ApoE-
/-.Chil3∆ and ApoE-/-.Chil3∆.hCHI3L2tg mice, while primary VSMCs were

Foam cell formation: BMDMs with different genotypes were treated with 50

from ApoE-/-.Chil3∆ BMDMs (Fig. 4b in this letter).
Calcification: BMDMs were cultured with ox-LDL and calcification medium for
10 days. Conditioned media applied to VSMCs for 14 days enhanced
calcification (Fig. 4a in this letter). Alizarin red staining demonstrated that,
relative to conditioned media from ApoE-/-.Chil3∆ BMDMs, media from ApoE-/-

The new results have been included in the revised manuscript as Fig. 3i-k.
Certainly, in addition to the autocrine regulatory effects of CLPs on
macrophages, their regulatory influences on other cell types, including VSMCs,
are also interesting and significant. While this study focuses on macrophages,
the mechanisms by which CLPs regulate VSMCs will be explored in future work.
Fig. 4. CLPs promote the phenotypic transformation of VSMCs.
5. Quantification of western blotting results is needed throughout the
manuscript (eg. Fig6b-d, …).
Answer: Thank you for your careful attention. We wish to clarify that Fig. 6b-d,
Fig. 7a-b, and Extended Data Fig. 6a in our manuscript present results from co-
immunoprecipitation (co-IP) experiments, not standard Western blotting
quantifying protein expression levels. Co-IP primarily demonstrates qualitative
protein-protein interactions: that is, whether one protein physically binds to
another. The data are typically presented as a pair of blots from the same
experiment: one showing the immunoprecipitated complex and another
showing the input controls. The presence or absence of a band, rather than its
intensity, indicates binding. Band intensity can be influenced by IP efficiency
and does not linearly reflect binding affinity.
Key co-IP experiments were independently replicated three times, with all
replicates consistently confirming the interaction pattern; representative blots
are shown in the manuscript. Furthermore, we confirm that all other Western
blotting images intended to show expression or activity levels have been
subjected to quantitative analysis. Detailed results are provided in Fig. 7, 8 and
Extended Data Fig. 1, 6, 8 of the revised manuscript.
6. In addition to CD36 and Abcg1, the protein expression levels of other lipid
uptake receptors (e.g., SR-B1, LDLR) and cholesterol efflux transporters (e.g.,
ABCA1) should be examined, as their expression may be influenced by post-
translational regulation. Assessing only mRNA levels by qRT-PCR is insufficient.

lipid uptake receptors (LDLR, MSR1, OLR1 and SR-B1) and core cholesterol

conditions via Western blotting (Fig. 5 in this letter). Key findings indicate that,

Fig. 5. The effect of CLPs on receptors involved in cholesterol metabolism.

1. While the manuscript is largely well-written, there are several instances of
the use of unusual terminology. For instance, the term "atherosclerogenesis" is
unusual. The commonly used term for this process is atherogenesis. In addition,

Answer: Thanks. We have revised the manuscript accordingly to adhere to the
common use.
 "Atherosclerogenesis" has been replaced with the standard and widely
accepted term "atherogenesis" throughout the manuscript.
 “Fate mapping” has been replaced with precise descriptions; we now
describe our data as revealing the “phenotypic transition” of cells (Lines
219-279 in the revised manuscript).
 The sentence structure has been corrected to the standard form, "...the
expression of CHI3L2 and CHI3L1 in macrophages was... (as shown in
lines 137-138 in the revised manuscript.)" (treating "expression" as a
singular entity), and we have carefully checked the entire text.
2.ORO and histological staining data in Fig. 1f, g, and i should be enlarged. There also appears to be a discrepancy in the

Answer: We apologize for the oversight in using representative image
presentation. We have now enlarged key histological images (Fig. 2c-f, 4, 9,
and Extended Data Fig. 2 in the revised manuscript, Fig. 1, 3 in this letter) to
better highlight cellular details. All scale bars have been carefully reviewed and
corrected to ensure accurate reporting. These updates have been incorporated
into the revised manuscript, and we sincerely appreciate your constructive
feedback.
3. The human plasma and tissue cohorts (n=34 healthy, n=38 atherosclerotic)
are modest. Excluding patients with diabetes/hypertension limits clinical
relevance, as these conditions frequently coexist with atherosclerosis. The
authors should address whether findings generalize to broader populations.
Answer: Thanks. We fully agree that the cohort size in this study is limited.
However, this research was designed as a mechanism-driven, proof-of-concept
investigation rather than a large-scale epidemiological study. Our primary goal
was to minimize confounding variables during the initial discovery phase to
obtain a clear, interpretable signal regarding the specific role of CHI3L2 in
atherosclerosis. Using a tightly controlled, focused cohort is a well-established
approach in early biomarker and mechanistic research, establishing
foundational insights before extending to larger, more heterogeneous
populations.
Given that diabetes and hypertension frequently coexist with atherosclerosis,
their exclusion was a deliberate methodological choice, allowing us to examine
the direct contribution of CHI3L2 without interference from strong confounding
signals associated with major metabolic and stress pathways. This controlled
design strengthens the internal validity of our study and increases confidence
that the observed associations are attributable to atherosclerosis itself rather
than secondary effects of hyperglycemia or hypertension.
In response to your concern, we have explicitly acknowledged this limitation in
the revised discussion section of the manuscript (Lines 688-695). Notably,
growing evidence suggests that the biological pathways examined in our study
may indeed be relevant to broader patient groups. For instance, CHI3L1 (YKL-
40) is established as a key mediator of inflammation and vascular pathology in
atherosclerosis, metabolic syndrome and diabetes4. This precedent offers a
strong biological rationale for hypothesizing that CHI3L2 may likewise play an
important role in populations with comorbidities. We are actively planning
follow-up translational clinical studies to test this hypothesis.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
In this study, Wang et al. reported the impact of Chitinase-like protein 3 (Chil3)
and its human functional homolog chitinase-3-like 2 (CHI3L2) on macrophage
lipid metabolism and atherosclerosis. Using numerous elegant experimental
approaches as well as in in vitro and in vivo models, the authors proposed a
new autocrine mechanism in which secreted CLP regulates cholesterol uptake
in macrophages through binding to CD36. Importantly, Wang et al. provided
important new therapeutic insights with the use of antibodies targeting CHI3L2
which attenuate atherosclerosis. This group previously demonstrated that Chil3
polymorphisms were associated with inflammatory diseases by regulating lipid
metabolism. This study is in the continuation of their previous works by
positioning Chil3 in the development of atherosclerosis. The overall study is
very interesting but several points must be clarified by the authors.
Major points.
1. Previous numerous studies characterized several macrophage populations
in atherosclerotic plaques by single-cell RNA-Sequencing (PMID: 38639096,
PMID: 29545366, PMID: 31591603, PMID: 32981416….). Was Chil3
expression associated with a specific subtype cluster of macrophages in
atherosclerotic plaques (Trem2+ macrophages (PMID: 38646596))? Was
this latter altered upon Chil3 deficiency? Analysis of Chil3 expression in CAM
(classically activated macrophages) and AAM (alternatively activated
macrophages) is indeed very limited (Extended Data Fig. 2e-h).
Answer: We thank you for the insightful comments. In our scRNA-seq dataset,
we identified seven macrophage subpopulations in atherosclerotic aortas:
Ly6C2+ monocyte-like, resident, MHC-II, inflammatory, foamy, VSMC-like, and
fibrochondrocyte (FC)-like macrophages. Chil3 was specifically enriched in
Ly6C2+ monocyte-like macrophages in ApoE-/- mice, whereas CHI3L2 was
mainly expressed in foam cells, VSMC-like macrophages, and FC-like
macrophages in ApoE-/-.Chil3∆.hCHI3L2tg mice. Functionally, Chil3 increased
inflammatory macrophages and reduced resident macrophages, while CHI3L2
expanded foam cell/FC-like clusters at the expense of resident and MHC-II
macrophages (Fig. 6 in this letter). These differences are consistent with the
fact that Chil3 and CHI3L2 are not direct orthologs and exhibit subtype-specific
patterns and consequences. The new results have been included in the revised
manuscript as Fig. 3d-f and Extended Data Fig. 3b.
Fig. 6. scRNA-seq analysis of aortic macrophage phenotyping across
three genotypes.
The Chil3+ macrophage population we identified co-expressed canonical Ly6C+
monocyte markers (Ly6c2, Ccr2, Ccl2) and inflammatory genes (Il1b, Ifitm
family), corresponding to a pro-inflammatory monocyte-like state similar to the
“monocyte-macrophage transitional state” described by Yang et al., who also
reported high Chil3 expression in this cluster5. In our model, Chil3 deficiency
did not markedly change this monocyte-like cluster but reduced inflammatory
macrophages and increased resident macrophages, consistent with prior
observations that Ly6Chi monocytes dominate healthy arteries, whereas
Ly6Clow monocytes predominate in atherosclerosis6.
These data suggest that Chil3’s effects on inflammatory and resident
macrophages, rather than monocyte-like cells, drive disease progression.
Although foam cell clusters were not significantly altered, foam cell formation
decreased, indicating that Chil3 regulates macrophage functional programs
rather than cluster identity.
Chil3’s role is context-dependent. In acute injury, Chil3 Ly6C monocytes are
immunoregulatory and pro-repair7, while in chronic inflammation such as
⁺ ⁺
atherosclerosis, Chil3 is expressed in pro-inflammatory Ly6C monocyte-
derived macrophages, and its deficiency attenuates plaque development. This
⁺
reflects the influence of the tissue microenvironment: acute injury fosters a
resolution-oriented milieu that permits Chil3+ monocytes to adopt reparative
programs, whereas the lipid-rich, oxidative, necrotic environment of
atherosclerotic plaques redirects these cells toward pro-inflammatory fates.
We also mapped CHI3L2 expression in atherosclerotic plaques. scRNA-seq
data show that macrophages are highly plastic8,9. Prior studies identified lipid-
poor inflammatory and Trem2 foam macrophages, with Trem2 cells linked to
advanced lesions10,11. Consistent with this, we identified a Trem2+ foam cell
⁺ ⁺
population (also called foamy macrophages in our revised Fig.3). CHI3L2 was
predominantly expressed within these late-stage Trem2+ foam cells, and its
expression greatly expanded this population in ApoE-/-.Chil3∆.hCHI3L2tg mice.
We have already covered this topic in the Discussion section (Lines 593-606).
Macrophage polarization experiments (Extended Data Fig.1g-j in the revised
manuscript) were performed not to replicate scRNA-seq clusters but to identify
the human functional homolog of mouse-specific Chil3. Using chromosomal
synteny and functional polarization assays, we found that CHI3L2, not CHI3L1,
aligns with Chil3: Chil3 and CHI3L2 are established markers of alternatively
activated macrophages (AAMs)12,13, whereas CHI3L1 is mainly associated with
classically activated macrophages (CAMs)14. These data support focusing on
the Chil3/CHI3L2 functional axis.
2. Because lipid uptake in macrophages has a profound impact on intracellular
lipid homeostasis beyond foam cell formation, it is important to further describe
the consequences of the alteration of Chil3 expression in the lipidome of
macrophages, especially in membrane lipid composition. Then, lipidome of WT
and Chil3∆ macrophages must be explored in order to decipher the role of Chil3
in macrophages. Such an analysis is even more essential since Chil3 deficiency
allows an increased expression of Abcg1, a transporter recently identified as
playing a key role in lipid rewiring and functions of macrophages (beyond
cholesterol efflux) (PMID: 39661702).
Answer: We sincerely appreciate your insightful suggestion. In response, we
performed non-targeted lipidomics on macrophages from ApoE-/-, ApoE-
/-.Chil3∆ and ApoE-/-.Chil3∆.hCHI3L2tg mice. Neutral lipids including cholesterol,
cholesteryl esters (CE), and saturated fatty acids (USFA) were significantly
reduced, consistent with the decreased lipid droplet formation and foam cell
tendency observed in our model (Fig. 7a in this letter). In contrast, membrane-
associated lipid species were markedly increased in ApoE-/-.Chil3∆
macrophages, including several classes of phospholipids
(Phosphatidylethanolamine (PE), Phosphatidylglycerol (PG),
Phosphatidylserine (PS), Phosphatidylinositol (PI)), lysophospholipids
(Lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC), Lysophosphatidylethanolamine (LPE)), and
sphingolipids (Ceramides (Cer)) (Fig. 7b in this letter). These findings indicate
that loss of CLPs drives a membrane-focused rewiring of lipid metabolism,
resulting in increased membrane lipid enrichment and altered biophysical
properties. These results have been added to the revised manuscript (Fig. 8b,
c).
Fig. 7. The effects of CLPs on macrophage lipids.
Dahik et al. reported impaired PE metabolism and reduced phosphatidylcholine
(PC) in ABCG1-deficient BMDMs15, consistent with our model in which CLP
expression suppresses ABCG1 and lowers these phospholipids. They also
showed that ABCG1 loss redistributes saturated fatty acids (SFA) from
membranes to lipid droplets, increasing USFA, decreasing membrane rigidity,
and reducing pro-inflammatory lipids15. Interestingly, in contrast, we observed
that CLPs (with low ABCG1) increase SFA, likely reflecting the context-
dependent role of ABCG116. In atherosclerosis, ABCG1 primarily facilitates
cholesterol transport, and its inhibition is pro-inflammatory17, whereas in
metabolic disease, it regulates fatty acid metabolism, where inhibition can be
anti-inflammatory15.
Our data indicate that CLPs broadly regulate membrane lipid distribution. While
our primary aim was to dissect how CLPs modulate cholesterol pathways via
the mTOR-PPARγ-ABCG1 axis, the lipidomic changes suggest CLPs may also
influence PPARγ indirectly through membrane composition. We propose that
loss of CLPs increases membrane phospholipids and sphingolipids, triggering
compensatory ABCG1 upregulation and reducing SFA and cholesterol,
establishing a distinct lipid-rewiring state that may further shape macrophage
inflammatory function. We now highlight in the revised Discussion (Lines 658–
666) that future studies should examine fatty acid saturation ratios, membrane
fluidity, lipid droplet dynamics, and ABCG1 inhibition consequences.
3. Through the uptake of oxidized lipids and free fatty acids, CD36 plays major
roles in several pathways controlling the metabolic phenotype of macrophage
(fatty acid oxidation and storage, ROS production, energy metabolism….). The
authors must provide information about the impact of Chil3 deficiency on
metabolic pathways in macrophages (RNA-sequencing and/or seahorse
analyses for example).
Answer: Thank you for your suggestion. Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA)
of differentially expressed genes in macrophages from scRNA-seq, revealed
that CLPs deficiency downregulated inflammation-related pathways, including
the NOD-like receptor, chemokine, and cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction
signaling pathway, while upregulating metabolism-related pathways such as
oxidative phosphorylation, PPAR signaling, and glutathione metabolism (Fig. 8
in this letter). This suggests that CLPs may be involved in regulating
macrophage inflammatory responses, energy metabolism, and antioxidant
capacity. In addition, the lysosome pathway was also markedly enhanced,
reflecting increased cellular degradation and recycling capacity in CLP-deficient
macrophages, which may indirectly support metabolic reprogramming and
energy supply (Fig. 8 in this letter). The supplementary results are presented
in Extended data Fig. 7a in the revised manuscript.
Fig. 8. GSEA analysis.
Research on the mechanisms linking CLPs to energy metabolism remains in
its early stages. This study primarily focused on identifying a novel mode of
action for CLPs: a protein exhibiting glycosidase-like hydrolytic activity that
regulates the N-glycosylation modification of CD36, along with its subsequent
role in the PPARγ-ABCG1 signaling pathway. Our current experiments
demonstrate CLPs' role in regulating obesity and non-alcoholic fatty liver
disease (NAFLD). Models of obesity and NAFLD effectively illustrate how CLPs
influence energy metabolism biological processes. Direct metabolic flux and
enzyme activity assays (e.g., via Seahorse analysis) will further elucidate these
mechanisms, which we plan to validate in subsequent work. However, the
primary focus of this paper remains the novel CLP receptor and its effects on
the receptor.
4. The authors did not explain and discuss the role of Chil3 on inflammation,
especially on the inflammatory phenotype of macrophages. Because CD36,
the main target of Chil3, is involved in NLRP3 activation (PMID: 23812099),
the reduced IL-1β expression observed in aorta of Chil3∆ mice (Fig1e) could
result from an impaired activation of the NLRP3 pathway. Although the role of
Chil3 in foam cell formation is very likely involved in the attenuated
atherosclerosis development, the authors cannot exclude the role of
inflammation in their mechanism since anti-inflammatory targeting IL-1β led to
a reduction of atherosclerotic cardiovascular diseases (PMID: 28845751). The
authors must explore and/or discuss this aspect.
Answer: Thanks. CD36-mediated lipid uptake promotes intracellular
cholesterol crystallization and activates the NLRP3 inflammasome, enhancing
IL-1β maturation and secretion18. As shown in Fig.8 of this letter, the NOD-like
signaling pathway was significantly upregulated in the presence of CLPs.
Further analysis showed that the core component of the NOD-like receptor
family, the pyrin domain-containing 3 (Nlrp3) inflammasome, was significantly
downregulated in macrophages from ApoE-/-.Chil3∆ mice, accompanied by
markedly reduced expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including Il1b, Il6
and Tnf (Fig. 9a in this letter). These results suggest that the inflammasome
may serve as a critical mediator through which CLPs regulate inflammatory
cytokine expression in macrophages. However, the expression of Il6 and Tnf
does not entirely depend on NLRP3 inflammasome activation19. RNA
sequencing also revealed a significant enrichment of inflammatory signaling
pathways (Fig. 9b in this letter). These results are presented in the Externed
Data Fig. 7b-d of the revised manuscript.
Fig. 9. The effects of CLPs on macrophage inflammation.
Integrating these data, we propose a “polarization-metabolic axis” model: Chil3
deficiency reduces CD36-mediated lipid uptake, decreases lysosomal lipid load,
and inhibits mTOR signaling. This shifts macrophages toward an anti-
inflammatory state, increasing PPARγ expression and enhancing ABCG1-
mediated cholesterol efflux (detailed explanation provided in responses to
Questions 15 and 16). The overall attenuation of pro-inflammatory
transcriptional programs (Fig. 9 in this letter) explains the coordinated
downregulation of Il1b, Il6 and Tnf. Previous studies show that CAMs provides
an “initiation signal” for inflammasome activation, whereas anti-inflammatory or
partially AAM-biased programs limit it20,21. Thus, reduced Nlrp3 expression in
Chil3-deficient macrophages reflects an overall shift toward an anti-
inflammatory state, and we highlight the potential role of inflammasome
signaling in the Discussion section (Lines 682-687).
Others major points.
5. In mice with a total Chil3 deficiency, what tissue drives the circulating Chil3 /
CHI3L2 concentrations in mice (Fig. 1a, Extended data Fig. 2i……)? Same
question in humans (Fig. 2c)?
Answer: Under physiological conditions, Chil3 is predominantly expressed in
macrophages of the lung, bone marrow, and spleen22, whereas CHI3L2 is
predominantly expressed in articular chondrocytes as well as lung and heart
macrophages23. Although their basal expression is low, both genes are
markedly upregulated in disease settings. In atherosclerosis models, we
propose that locally recruited macrophages are the primary source driving the
increase in circulating Chil3 (CHI3L2). Numerous studies have shown that
activated macrophages are the major source of CLPs under inflammatory
conditions14. Our scRNA-seq data reveal that Chil3 expression predominantly
arises from monocyte-derived macrophage subsets, whereas CHI3L2
expression is largely confined to late-stage macrophages (Fig. 6 in this letter).
These macrophages may undergo apoptosis during atherosclerosis
progression, potentially releasing their CLP content into the circulation.
Accordingly, we infer that circulating CHI3L2 in humans is also primarily derived
from inflammatory macrophages involved in atherosclerotic lesions. While
plaque macrophages represent the main source, other tissues such as Kupffer
cells in the liver and macrophages in adipose tissue may also contribute
modestly in a systemic inflammatory context, as we observed that CLPs also
affect obesity and NAFLD.
6. Extended Data Fig. 1(a). What was the diet of ApoE-/- and WT mice ?
Answer: All mice were maintained on a normal diet (ND) for 32 weeks. To
examine CLP family expression, ApoE-/- mice on ND or WD would normally be
selected. We reviewed numerous GEO datasets of mouse atherosclerosis
models (ApoE-/- on ND or WD), but large-scale detection of CLP family genes
(Chil1, Chil3, Chil4, Chid1 and Ovgp1) was largely undetectable, likely due to
they are secreted proteins and mRNA levels are relatively low. In the GSE2372
dataset24, all screened CLP family members were detectable; this dataset
includes ApoE-/-and WT mice on ND at 32 weeks. Given that ApoE-/- mice on
ND can spontaneously develop atherosclerosis by this age, we used them as
the model group, with WT mice as controls. Notably, GSE2372 had a small
sample size (n=3), so we integrated it with another public dataset,
GSE20741425, which includes ApoE-/- and WT mice on ND for 40 weeks and is
comparable to GSE2372 (Fig. 10 in this letter, Extended Data Fig. 1a, b in the
revised manuscript).
Fig. 10. Expression of CLPs in mice and humans in the GEO dataset.
7. Fig. 1c. The title of the Y-axis must be clarified. What class of lipid was
quantified ? Cholesterol ? How was quantified the
lipid profile? How do the authors explain the reduced serum LDL (likely LDL-C) in BQ.ApoE-/-.Chil3-/- mice in comparison to
BQ.ApoE-/- mice ? Same comments in Fig. 2e).
Answer: Sorry. We have modified the Y-axis label to define it as lipid
(cholesterol & TG) profiles in serum (mmol/L). HDL and LDL should also be
replaced with HDL-C and LDL-C, because the test measures cholesterol in
these components (Fig. 11 in this letter). As stated in the manuscript, plasma
lipid levels were measured using a direct homogeneous assay on a Beckman
AU5431 automatic biochemistry analyzer, which employs specific surfactants
and enzymes to quantify cholesterol primarily within the HDL/LDL fraction. We
have changed all instances of HDL or LDL in the revised manuscript to HDL-C
or LDL-C (Fig. 2a, b).
Fig. 11. lipid (cholesterol & TG) profiles in serum (mmol/L). TC, total
cholesterol; TG, triglyceride; LDL-C, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol;
HDL-C, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol.
Inflammation could be a key driver of hepatic VLDL (a precursor to LDL in
circulation), and decreased inflammation may reduce VLDL/LDL production26,27.
We have found that Chil3 deficiency significantly attenuates both local and
systemic inflammation (Fig. 8, 9 in this letter), which may explain the reduced
LDL-C levels in mice. In addition, downregulation of systemic inflammation may
also improve hepatic lipid metabolism, enabling the liver to more effectively
clear circulating LDL. Our recent study on CLPs in NFLAD showed that CLPs
significantly reduced hepatic lipid deposition, suggesting that CLP deficiency
contributes to improved hepatic lipid metabolism. However, more observations
are still required in future in this study to ascertain the conclusive roles and
mechanisms.
8. Same question with oxLDL (Fig. 1d).
Answer: We propose several potential mechanisms: (1) Reduced oxidative
environment for ox-LDL generation. In atherosclerosis, ox-LDL generation is
driven by inflammation-induced oxidative stress. Chil3 deficiency markedly
attenuates systemic and lesion-associated inflammation (Fig. 8, 9 in this
letter), lowering oxidative conditions necessary for LDL modification and
reducing ox-LDL production. (2) Reduced hepatic VLDL/LDL secretion leading
to a smaller LDL substrate pool. As noted above, Chil3 deficiency may impair
the liver’s capacity to secrete VLDL, decreasing circulating LDL levels and
consequently limiting the substrate available for oxidative modification. (3)
Potential enhancement of antibody-mediated clearance of ox-LDL. Natural
antibodies in the circulation can bind ox-LDL to form immune complexes, which
are then efficiently cleared by macrophages in the liver and spleen28. Chil3
deficiency may indirectly improve the efficiency of this immunological clearance
pathway. (4) More efficient non-pathological clearance of ox-LDL. ox-LDL may
also be removed through more effective, non-inflammatory scavenger
pathways. For example, functional macrophages or hepatic Kupffer cells may
clear ox-LDL more efficiently through alternative receptors without becoming
lipid-overloaded, as Chil3 deficiency improves hepatic immunometabolic
homeostasis. Notably, several of these mechanisms are supported by our
independent research demonstrating that CLP deficiency improves hepatic lipid
homeostasis, but more work is still needed to understand these mechanisms.
9. Fig. 2k. The efficiency of the treatment with rhCHI3L2 must be validated by
quantification of CHI3L2 in the circulation of mice following intraperitoneal
injection.
Answer: Thanks. We assessed circulating CHI3L2 levels following
intraperitoneal injection of an hIgG1-Fc-tagged rhCHI3L2, which was designed
to extend its plasma half-life in vivo. Two-month-old ApoE-/-.Chil3∆ mice were
fed a WD for 1 month before initiating protein administration. During the
subsequent 2 months of WD feeding, mice received intraperitoneal injections
every three days of either hFc-rhCHI3L2 (0.25 µg/g) or an hFc-IgG1 control
(0.25 µg/g). Serum collected on days 2 and 3 post-injection was analyzed using
a commercial ELISA kit, and we found that serum CHI3L2 levels on day 2 post-
injection reached 35.64% of initial treatment containing 0.50 µg/mL CHI3L2
protein. By day 3, the level decreased to 12.85%. No detectable CHI3L2 signal
was observed in the control group on day 2 (Fig. 12 in this letter). This
confirms that our intraperitoneal delivery protocol successfully introduces the
recombinant protein into the systemic circulation, supporting the biological
relevance of the observed phenotypic effects. We have referenced the newly
added supplementary data in the Results section (Extended Data Fig. 2b).
Fig. 12. Validation of recombinant protein injection into the body.
10. Fig. 3. Single-cell RNA-Sequencing data are interesting but it would be
useful to know the biological pathways that are altered in macrophages in the
three mouse models (WT, Chil3∆ and Chil3∆.CHI3L2tg). A same comment can
be done in BMDM and PM cells (Fig. 5). As a whole, impact of Chil3 deletion
as well as expression of CHI3L2 in Chil3-deficient cells on the metabolic
phenotype of macrophages is lacking. In this context, it is very intriguing that
no cholesterol metabolism (or lipid metabolism) pathways were found altered
by RNA-sequencing in ox-LDL stimulated Chil3∆ versus WT BMDM
(Extended Data Fig. 7b). These findings weaken a significant role of Chil3 in
macrophage lipid uptake as proposed by the authors.
Answer: The scRNA-seq results are shown in Fig.8 of this letter. We
reanalyzed the RNA-seq data, focusing on gene sets related to cholesterol
metabolism, and observed upregulation of key genes regulating intracellular
cholesterol processing in ox-LDL-stimulated ApoE-/-.Chil3Δ BMDMs: including
Npc1, Npc2 (lysosomal cholesterol efflux), Stard3 (lysosomal-endoplasmic
reticulum cholesterol transport), Lipa (lysosomal cholesterol esterification),
Nceh1 (cytoplasmic cholesterol esterification), Soat1 (Acat1) (cholesterol re-
esterification), Abcg1 (cholesterol efflux). In contrast, changes in cholesterol
uptake and biosynthesis genes were minimal (Fig. 13 in this letter). This
pattern suggests that Chil3 deficiency promotes rapid lysosomal cholesterol
efflux, efficient cholesterol esterification, and enhanced delivery of cholesterol
efflux mechanisms such as ABCG1. These results are presented in Extended
Data Fig. 8 of the revised manuscript.
Fig. 13. RNA-seq data.
11. Fig. 6. Although not in the top 5 candidate, were P2Y6R and TREM2 (or
some TLRs) identified in IP and MS analyses since these receptors promote
lipid uptake and atherosclerosis (PMID: 38036416, PMID: 38646596)?
Answer: We appreciate your insightful question. As highlighted in the
suggested references, P2RY6 and TREM2 are recognized promoters of lipid
uptake and atherosclerosis3,11. In our IP-MS analysis aimed at identifying high-
confidence Chil3-interacting proteins, neither receptor appeared in statistically
significant matches, indicating that under our experimental conditions, they do
not form stable or direct complexes with Chil3 detectable by this method. While
exploring additional potential receptors is scientifically valuable, the primary
goal of this study was to move from large-scale screening to mechanistic
validation. CD36 emerged as the top candidate in our IP-MS screen, guiding us
to focus subsequent functional experiments on this high-probability target. This
approach allowed us to rigorously demonstrate that CLPs (Chil3 and CHI3L2)
directly bind CD36, remodel its N-glycans, and thereby enhance CD36-
mediated lipid uptake, a pathway critical for in vivo atherosclerosis development.
CD36 thus serves as a clear example to elucidate the novel mechanism of
CLPs in atherosclerosis.
We have not excluded the involvement of other receptors. As stated, “Although
we did not observe any interaction between CLPs and the scavenger receptors
OLR1 and MSR1, the possibility of their interactions cannot be ruled out” (Fig.
6b in the revised manuscript, Discussion section, Lines 610-611). Current data
do not support direct interactions between Chil3 and P2RY6 or TREM2, but
indirect effects or context-dependent interactions remain possible. Investigating
additional CLP-associated receptors represents an important direction for
future research.
12. As a follow up of my previous comment, may Chil3 promote hydrolysis of
N-glycosylated glycans of others membrane proteins without physically
interacting with them (and then not to be detected by co-IP)?
Answer: The possibility you raise is plausible. Lectin-glycan interactions are
inherently transient, so Chil3 could theoretically act on other glycoproteins after
modifying CD36. However, Chil3’s three-dimensional structure restricts binding
to specific glycan conformations; if other membrane proteins do not present
compatible glycans, Chil3 will not engage or act on them29.
Our functional data indicate that CD36 is the primary target of Chil3 in
atherosclerosis models, likely due to its highest affinity for CD36’s specific
glycan structure. If Chil3 broadly hydrolyzed N-glycans across many membrane
proteins, we would expect widespread effects on multiple receptors. Instead,
we observe a highly specific phenotype: impaired CD36-mediated lipid uptake
without significant changes in other scavenger receptor functions. This supports
a specific regulatory role via the Chil3-CD36 axis rather than broad, non-
specific glycan remodeling.
While broader substrate activity cannot be entirely excluded, we are planning
in vitro glycan array and cryo-electron microscopy analyses to systematically
define its complete enzymatic substrate spectrum30. Within this study,
combined genetic, biochemical, and functional evidence confirms the Chil3-
CD36 axis as a key pathway in macrophage lipid metabolism and
atherosclerosis.
13. Fig. 8a. How do the authors explain that the impaired cholesterol uptake in
Chil3∆ BMDM was not accompanied by an increased expression of Ldlr and
Hmgcr genes; the expression of these genes being downregulated by
cholesterol.
Answer: In classical cholesterol homeostasis, reduced intracellular cholesterol
upregulates LDLR and HMGCR via SREBP2 activation31. This represents a
crucial feedback regulatory mechanism for maintaining cellular cholesterol
homeostasis. However, in ApoE-/- and ApoE-/-.Chil3∆ BMDMs with or without ox-
LDL stimulation, we found that Ldlr/Hmgcr were downregulated compared to
their respective controls. Yet, no differences in Ldlr/Hmgcr expression were
observed among the two genotypes after ox-LDL treatment (Fig. 14 in this
letter). We propose that ox-LDL-stimulated BMDMs represent a foam cell
model, where high ox-LDL exposure causes substantial intracellular cholesterol
accumulation, creating a “cholesterol overload” state. In this context, SREBP2
activity is suppressed by intracellular cholesterol, as reflected by
downregulated Ldlr and Hmgcr in all ox-LDL-treated BMDMs (Fig. 14 in this
letter). This confirms that the classical cholesterol feedback pathway is
inhibited under foam cell conditions.
Fig. 14. The expression of cholesterol-related molecules.
Thus, the key question is not why Chil3 deficiency fails to upregulate Ldlr/Hmgcr,
but how it still reshapes macrophage cholesterol metabolism under cholesterol
overload. Our data show that Chil3-deficient macrophages reduce net
cholesterol accumulation by two mechanisms: limiting CD36-mediated uptake
and enhancing the PPARγ-ABCG1 efflux axis. This positions Chil3 as a critical
cholesterol “fine-tuner,” regulating a pathway that can override the classical
SREBP2 feedback. Even when SREBP2 is suppressed, Chil3 specifically
balances cholesterol import (CD36) and export (ABCG1).
Additionally, upregulation of the E3 ligase Mylip in Chil3-deficient macrophages
promotes LDLR degradation32, explaining why LDLR levels remain unchanged
despite reduced uptake (Fig. 13 in this letter).
14. Fig. 8d. Although the method used to quantify cholesterol efflux is highly
questionable, the results are quite intriguing. Indeed, a 45% cholesterol efflux
during a 4h incubation with HDL is extremely high (about 10% is expected) and
suggests an alteration of cell viability. The authors must describe the method
used (what type of HDL used? what is the % of
cholesterol efflux without
HDL ? ……..).
Answer: The cholesterol efflux assay was performed following the
manufacturer's instructions (ab196985; Abcam). Macrophages were seeded in
96-well plates (1×10⁵ cells/well), loaded with fluorescent-labeled cholesterol at
37°C for 1 h, incubated for 16 h, and then treated with serum-free medium
containing HDL (ApoB-depleted serum) for 4 h. Fluorescence of supernatant
and cell lysates were measured (Ex/Em = 485/523 nm, Infinite M200, Tecan).
Culture medium and cell lysate cholesterol efflux were calculated based on the
fluorescence intensity of the medium and that of cell lysates, in accordance with
the manufacturer’s instructions (Methods section, Lines 910-918).
We fully understand your concerns regarding the relatively high cholesterol
efflux rate (45%) observed in our experiments, which indeed exceeds the
approximately 10% typically reported using conventional radiolabeling methods.
However, we wish to clarify that this result is consistent with the data range
reported in multiple published studies using the same fluorescent assay kit we
employed33-35. Under similar conditions (HDL acceptor, 4 h incubation),
reported efflux rates range 30-50%. This is not an anomaly but a characteristic
of this methodology. HDL-mediated cholesterol efflux capacity (CEC) can
prevent cardiovascular disease. However, the lack of standardization in CEC
assays hinders their application in large cohorts and comparability across
studies. Cell-based CEC assays are influenced by numerous factors:
cholesterol donor cells, cholesterol tracers, and HDL samples36,37.
Two main CEC assay methods exist: BODIPY-cholesterol consistently shows
higher efflux than [³H]-cholesterol: 11.8 ± 0.6%/h vs. 2.7 ± 0.3%/h with 2%
apoB-depleted serum, reflecting its higher sensitivity and suitability for high-
throughput screening to link cholesterol efflux with atherosclerosis38.
15. Extended Data Fig. 7d and Figure 8. The authors proposed that the increased
Abcg1 expression resulted from an elevation of Ppar expression. If it is the case,
Abca1 expression would be also increased since induction of Ppar stimulates
Abca1 expression (PMID: 11135616)
Answer: In exploring how CLPs (Chil3 and CHI3L2) regulate macrophage lipid
homeostasis, we observed that CLP deficiency reduces lipid uptake while
promoting lipid efflux. RT-qPCR and Western blotting of macrophages under
ox-LDL stimulation showed that among efflux receptors, only ABCG1 was
significantly upregulated, while ABCA1 remained unchanged in CLP-deficient
cells (Fig. 14, 15a in this letter), indicating CLPs primarily rely on the ABCG1
mediated cholesterol efflux pathway. Cholesterol uptake and synthesis-related
molecules showed no significant differences across groups (Fig. 14, 15a in this
letter).
We previously found that Chil3 deficiency upregulates PPARγ in pneumonia
and psoriasis mouse models12,39. Here, under ox-LDL, CLP deficiency also
increased PPARγ expression, and PPARγ inhibitors reversed ABCG1
upregulation and lipid reduction, confirming its central role (Fig. 16 in this
letter).The physiological ligand of PPARγ, ox-LDL, activates ligand-dependent
transcription40. However, when CLPs are absent, lipid intake decreases and the
increased PPARγ does not have sufficient ligands to activate it, suggesting a
ligand-independent signaling. PPARγ expression levels can also be modulated
by microenvironmental cues such as proinflammatory cytokines, leading to
alterations in PPARγ-mediated events through a ligand-independent pathway12.
Our study reveals the existence of the ligand-independent PPARγ
transcriptional activation mechanism involving mTOR, a key regulator of lipid
metabolism and lipogenesis41.
Although classical PPARγ signaling involves the LXRα-ABCA1 axis42, studies
show that it can also regulate cholesterol efflux via ABCA1-independent
pathways43. Although ABCG1 and ABCA1 are both LXRα target genes, their
sensitivities to different signals, lipid environments, and transcription factor
combinations are distinct. One study demonstrated that PPARγ agonists
suppress foam cell formation without altering LXRα or ABCA1 expression43,
providing a plausible mechanism for the effects on LXR-independent and LXR-
dependent macrophage foam cell formation44.
RT-qPCR showed a trend toward increased Abca1 expression in ApoE-/- or
ApoE-/-.Chil3∆ BMDMs compared to their respective controls (without ox-LDL).
However, in Western blotting, ABCA1 protein expression in each genotype
showed no change after ox-LDL treatment compared to the untreated group
(Fig. 14, 15a in this letter), suggesting in the ox-LDL-stimulated foam cell
model, ABCA1 protein may undergo complex post-translational regulation,
such as ubiquitination or lysosomal degradation. Furthermore, LXRα
expression showed no significant changes, indicating that the classical LXRα-
ABCA1 axis was not effectively activated (Fig. 15b in this letter).
Heterogeneity in LXRα and ABCA1 expression may result from foam cells
accumulating high ox-LDL, which can suppress LXRα expression or promoter
activity and limit ABCA1 protein changes45. Alternatively, foam cell-like
macrophages may increase phagocytosis, removing LXRα agonists45.
Fig. 15. The expression of cholesterol-related molecules.
In summary, our model does not overturn classical theory but complements it
by revealing a refined transcriptional program in CLP-deficient macrophages.
Here, enhanced PPARγ signaling specifically upregulates ABCG1 via an LXR-
independent pathway. This section has been updated in the Results and
Discussion (Fig. 8a and Extended Data Fig. 8a–d, line 651-658 in the revised
manuscript).
16. Figures 8e-g. It is difficult to conclude on these experiments in the absence
of the WT BMDM. More importantly, the authors proposed that the reduced
cholesterol uptake (in the presence of ox-LDL) in Chil3∆ BMDM increases
Abcg1 expression through alteration of mTOR and induction of Ppar expression.
Such a mechanism is not coherent with the fact that oxysterols are potent
activators of Abcg1 expression through the LXR pathway (PMID: 16024918).
Indeed, Abcg1 expression is increased when macrophages are incubated with
ox-LDL (source of oxysterols) as confirmed in Fig. 8e-f. Then, it would be
expected to observe a reduced Abcg1 expression in Chil3∆ BMDM as a
consequence of the impaired ox-LDL uptake. How do the authors reconcile
these potential conflicting observations?
Answer: We appreciate your insightful comment. In the original manuscript,
signaling pathway studies were conducted in two main groups: Chil3-deficient
(ApoE-/-.Chil3∆) macrophages and their controls (ApoE-/-); CHI3L2 transgenic
(ApoE-/-.Chil3∆.hCHI3L2tg) macrophages and their controls (ApoE-/-.Chil3∆),
following strict littermate principles. During revision, we combined BMDMs from
all three littermate strains for Western blotting analysis, providing a more
intuitive presentation (Fig. 16 in this letter).
To elucidate CLPs’ direct mechanisms, we performed IP-MS, identifying CD36
as a receptor target. Functional experiments confirmed that CLPs specifically
hydrolyze CD36 N-glycans, enhancing CD36-mediated lipid uptake. This
represents the most significant innovation in our work: proposing a novel
biological function for CLPs: glycosidase-like activity.
Up-taken lipids enter endosomes, dissociate from CD36 in the acidic
environment, and are delivered to lysosomes for degradation46. These free
lipids (particularly cholesterol) are subsequently sensed in the lysosomal lumen
via well-established mechanisms involving the lysosomal cholesterol transport
complex (NPC1/NPC2) and the v-ATPase-Ragulator-Rag GTPase axis47-49.
Nutrients generated by lysosomal degradation (such as carbohydrates, lipids,
and amino acids) have been demonstrated to activate mTOR50-52. In this study,
we propose that exogenous lipids (especially ox-LDL) are the primary drivers
of mTOR activation in macrophages. Our data shows that compared to ApoE-
/-.Chil3∆ BMDMs, excessive ox-LDL significantly induced mTOR activation in
ApoE-/- and ApoE-/-.Chil3∆.hCHI3L2tg BMDMs. This mTOR activation was
completely eliminated when lysosomal acidification and function are specifically
inhibited using Bafilomycin A1 (Baf-A1) (Fig. 16a in this letter). This critical
finding underscores the absolute necessity of functional lysosomes in
transmitting ox-LDL-driven mTOR signaling.
Under ox-LDL stimulation, CLPs deficiency significantly increases PPARγ-
mediated lipid efflux (Fig. 16b in this letter), reflecting a non-ligand-dependent
PPARγ pathway. The relatively minor ox-LDL activation of PPARγ caused by
CLPs deficiency would be insufficient to follow a ligand-dependent PPARγ
pathway. PPARγ drives macrophage polarization independently of ligands, and
the IL-4/STAT6 axis promotes PPARγ expression and AAM-associated gene
transcription53-55. This indicates that PPARγ upregulation under AAMs
conditions is a common and conserved phenomenon53,54. These findings
collectively explain why CLPs deficiency induces a non-ligand-dependent
PPARγ pathway in macrophages, consistent with AAMs. In our atherosclerosis
research, we found that the presence of CLPs significantly increases the
expression of inflammatory cytokines such as Il1b, Il6 and Tnf in macrophage-
like foam cells, indicating an increased proportion of pro-inflammatory
macrophages (Fig. 16c in this letter).
mTORC1 nutrient sensing plays a key role in macrophage polarization,
promoting CAM activation56. Within CAMs, hypoxia inducible factor 1 alpha
(HIF-1α), which can be activated by mTORC1, is essential for the transcription
of proinflammatory cytokine genes57. Concurrently, high-protein diet-induced
atherosclerosis relies on macrophage mTORC158, and lysosomal cholesterol
loading independently activates mTORC159,60. As a negative regulator of AAMs,
Chil3 deficiency enhances the AAM phenotype12. Consistently, mTOR inhibitor
rapamycin reverses CLP-induced pro-inflammatory macrophage increases
(Fig. 16c in this letter) and upregulates PPARγ and ABCG1 in ApoE-/- and
ApoE-/-.Chil3∆.hCHI3L2tg macrophages (Fig. 16d in this letter).
The new results have been included in the revised manuscript as Fig. 8 and
Discussion (Lines 667-681).
Fig. 16. CLPs inhibit PPARγ-mediated cholesterol efflux through
activating mTOR signaling pathway.
Therefore, allow us to reiterate our proposed mechanism. CLPs target and
hydrolyze CD36 N-glycans, enhancing CD36-mediated ox-LDL uptake. At this
point, ox-LDL entering the lysosomes activates mTOR, reducing anti-
inflammatory macrophages and PPARγ expression via a ligand-insensitive
mechanism. This triggers a non-LXR-dependent decrease in ABCG1-mediated
cholesterol efflux. The combined effects of increased uptake and reduced efflux
drive macrophage lipid overload, promoting foam cell formation.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
This study focuses on the role of chitinase-like proteins in atherosclerosis.
Major:
1) General: how is LDL-cholesterol measured? This usually does not
accumulate at high levels in the plasma of ApoE-/-mice. The authors need to be
far more thorough here, especially since they state that they find differences.
Answer: We thank you for this insightful comment. Plasma LDL-C was
measured using a direct homogeneous assay on a Beckman AU5431 analyzer,
which quantifies cholesterol primarily in the LDL fraction. We fully acknowledge
your accurate point that the ApoE-/- mouse model is characterized primarily by
the accumulation of cholesterol-rich VLDL and remnant lipoproteins, and that
classic LDL is not the dominant fraction in the plasma of these mice under
standard conditions61. However, it is important to note that the "LDL-C" value
obtained from such direct homogeneous assays in dyslipidemia models like the
ApoE-/- mouse often captures not only true LDL but also a portion of the
cholesterol present in small, dense, atherogenic remnant lipoproteins that fall
within the measurable size/density range of the assay. Therefore, in the context
of our study, the reported "LDL-C" is best interpreted as a practical and widely
accepted index of the total atherogenic lipoprotein burden that is responsive to
experimental interventions, rather than solely the concentration of classic LDL
particles.
In response, we revised the Methods section(Lines 768-771) to clarify that “LDL
detection in ApoE-/ mice may include cholesterol from both classic LDL as well
as small, dense, atherogenic remnant lipoproteins, and thus serves as a
functional index of total atherogenic lipoprotein burden.” The significant
difference in LDL-C we observed strongly suggests that CLPs effectively
modulated this broader atherogenic lipoprotein pool (Fig. 17a in this letter).
This is a biologically relevant and meaningful finding. Our interpretation is
consistent with numerous studies in the field that report and discuss changes
in "LDL-C" measured by direct assays in ApoE-/- mice. For example: Xin-Yu
Yang et al. reported a significant decrease in plasma LDL-C in ApoE-/- mice
after hydroxyurea therapy, using a comparable direct method62.
Although our method does not distinguish classic LDL-C from dense remnants,
we further investigated lipoprotein atherogenicity by measuring plasma ox-LDL
using a highly specific and sensitive commercial ELISA kit (Novus Biologicals,
NBP3-18035). This method directly quantifies the oxidized lipoproteins, which
are the key drivers of foam cell formation and atherosclerosis progression. Our
data revealed that CLPs specifically promote the oxidation of atherogenic
lipoproteins (which reside within the broader "LDL-C" measurable pool). This
oxidation process is a central mechanism in atherosclerosis progression (Fig.
17b in this letter).
Fig. 17. Lipid level in mouse sera.
2) The authors several times refer to WT mice. It is well known that WT mice
do not develop atherosclerosis, so it does not make sense that atherosclerosis
would be studied in this particular model. The authors need to clarify this for
each and every study. Fig 2k-m. Were these wild-type mice? Or Ldlr-/- mice?
This needs to be clarified in the text. Line 207. Again, I am confused as to the
mouse models here. WT mice do not develop atherosclerosis. The authors
need to really clarify this better. Fig 4c-g. What was the genotype of the

regarding “WT” mice. In our study, all mice used for atherosclerosis

CHI3L2 gene. We fully agree that the use of "WT" in this context was imprecise
and could be misinterpreted as referring to the overall mouse model. To resolve
this unambiguously, we have now revised the entire manuscript accordingly.
The term "WT, Chil3∆ and Chil3∆.CHI3L2tg" has been replaced with the precise
genotype designation: "ApoE-/-, ApoE-/-.Chil3∆ and ApoE-/-.Chil3∆.CHI3L2tg".

to be at least n=10. In very many Figures, these numbers are lower; real
