Answer: Our animal experiments used inbred mice, with all experimental mice
having the same genetic background, and strictly followed the principle of
littermate controls to minimize variability within groups. We fully agree that the
necessary number of animals per group in experiments is required to ensure
accuracy of results, but it is also necessary to balance the 3R principles.
We have now expanded sample sizes to n ≥ 10 per group for all key
atherosclerosis analyses. The updated results, now included in Fig. 18-20, 33
below in this letter, robustly confirm our original conclusions. With this increased
sample size, the difference in lesion size between mice lacking CLPs and those
expressing CLPs remains highly statistically significant. All relevant figures,
statistical analyses, and the Methods section have been updated accordingly
in the revised manuscript. The new results have been included in the revised
manuscript as Fig. 1, 4, 9 and Extended Data Fig. 2.
Fig. 18. CLPs promote the formation of atherosclerosis.
Fig. 19. CHI3L2 recombinant proteins promote the formation of
atherosclerosis.
Fig. 20. Neutralizing CHI3L2 could block the progression of
atherosclerosis.
4) The authors need to provide more definitive evidence, preferably in vivo, that
the upregulation of CD36 is what accounts for their phenotype. Was CD36
staining increased in atherosclerotic plaques?
Answer: Our data indicate that the observed phenotype is driven not by
increased CD36 expression but by CLP-mediated post-translational
modification enhancing CD36-dependent lipid internalization. As macrophage-
secreted proteins, CLPs likely act in an autocrine manner.
Using IP-MS, we identified and validated a direct interaction between CLPs and
CD36. Total CD36 protein levels remained unchanged, indicating increased ox-
LDL uptake is not due to elevated biosynthesis (Fig. 21a in this letter).
Previous studies have demonstrated that CD36 levels on the cell membrane
decrease during lipid endocytosis2. To investigate this, we used flow cytometry
to assess CD36 levels on the cell surface of primary macrophages from mice
of different genotypes (with or without ox-LDL). A reduction in CD36 levels on
the cell membrane would indicate increased internalization of CD36, and
consequently, more intracellular lipid uptake2. Our results show that CLPs
induce a decrease in CD36 levels on the membrane surface, suggesting they
enhance the endocytosis of CD36 (Fig. 21b, c in this letter).
Immunofluorescence co-staining with the early endosome marker EEA1
confirmed increased CD36-EEA1 colocalization in Chil3-expressing cells,
providing direct evidence that CLPs promote CD36 trafficking into early
endosomes (Fig. 21d in this letter).
Fig. 21. CLPs affect CD36 endocytosis.
Of particular significance is our discovery of a glycosyltransferase-like function
for CLPs. Building on the lectin-like properties of the CLP family, we established
that their binding to CD36 is N-glycan-dependent. Label-free intact
glycopeptide mass spectrometry revealed that recombinant CLPs (rCLPs)
significantly reduce N-glycosylation at CD36 residues N220 and N321 (Fig. 22a
in this letter). To determine the functional relevance of these sites, we
generated CD36 expression vectors carrying glycosylation-site mutations and
transfected them into 293T cells. Compared with the wild-type construct, both
the single-point mutant CD36N220Q and the double mutant CD36N220Q-N321Q
exhibited enhanced ox-LDL uptake (Fig. 22b, c in this letter). Moreover, rCLPs
treatment enhanced lipid uptake only in wild-type CD36-expressing cells, with
no effect in mutants lacking the N220 and N321 glycosylation sites (Fig. 22b, c
in this letter). These findings delineate a finely-tuned regulatory mechanism
that will be the central subject of our ongoing and future investigations.
Accordingly, a primary and immediate objective is the generation of mouse
models carrying targeted mutations at the critical glycosylation sites (N220 and
N321) of CD36, which we anticipate will provide definitive in vivo validation of
the pathway uncovered here.
Fig. 22. CLPs affect the glycosylation of CD36.
5) Extended Data Fig 1a. These data on Chil3 being upregulated are not that
convincing. I understand the use of public datasets, which in general makes
things easier, but it seems to me that the n would need to be increased to really
conclude that Chil1 and Chid1 are not affected. These experiments are not hard
to do and would need to be performed in order for the authors to really draw
conclusions here.
Answer: We agree that drawing conclusive findings requires adequate sample
sizes. In the revised manuscript, we have strengthened our initial findings by
integrating two independent public datasets, which together provided a
combined sample size of n=7 (Extended Data Fig. 1a, b in the revised
manuscript). This integrated analysis revealed significant upregulation of Chil1,
Chil3, and Chid1 in CLP-enriched atherosclerotic aortas of mice (Fig. 23a in
this letter). Cross-referencing human atherosclerosis databases further
confirmed notable upregulation of CHI3L1 and CHI3L2 in human coronary
atherosclerotic plaques (Fig. 23b in this letter). These consistent findings
across species guided our focus toward these differentially expressed CLPs.
Fig. 23. CLPs levels in public RNA-seq dataset.
In determining our research focus, we considered several factors regarding
Chid1/CHID1:
 Its expression shows notable inter-species heterogeneity between mice
and humans
 The upregulation observed in murine atherosclerosis was relatively
modest compared to other CLPs (only 1.29-fold, whereas Chil1 and
Chil3 are upregulated by 8.78-fold and 4.94-fold, respectively)
 Existing literature coverage of Chid1 in CLP family studies remains
limited
 Chil1 (CHI3L1), Chil3, and CHI3L2 are the most widely distributed and
best characterized members of the CLP family, whereas research on
Chid1/CHID1 remains extremely limited
 Our primary objective is to prioritize these common CLPs, subsequently
applying insights analogously to all altered CLP molecules.
Our study was initially motivated by mouse Chil3, which previous research has
shown to influence alternative macrophage activation through regulation of lipid
metabolism12. This led us to hypothesize that Chil3 might play a role in lipid
metabolism disorders such as atherosclerosis. This prediction was
subsequently confirmed by our expanded research findings.
As Chil3 is mouse-specific, identifying its functional human homolog was
essential. Analysis of human atherosclerosis transcriptomic data revealed
significant overexpression of both CHI3L1 and CHI3L2 in atherosclerotic
plaques (Fig. 23b in this letter). Subsequent chromosomal synteny analysis
and macrophage polarization experiments demonstrated that CHI3L2, rather
than CHI3L1, exhibits a functional pattern in macrophage polarization that
closely mirrors that of mouse Chil3. This functional distinction is well-supported
in the literature: both Chil3 and CHI3L2 are established markers of alternatively
activated macrophages (AAMs)12,13, while CHI3L1 is predominantly associated
with classically activated macrophages (CAMs)14. Therefore, we focused
specifically on the functional axis comprising mouse Chil3 and human CHI3L2.
Indeed, the roles of CLPs in atherosclerosis remain poorly explored. Only a
handful of studies have suggested that Chil1 exacerbates atherosclerosis by
influencing macrophage apoptosis, endothelial inflammation, and vascular
smooth muscle cell activation63,64. Thus, our identification
of Chil3 and CHI3L2 represents the first evidence for the involvement of CLP
family members beyond Chil1 in this disease. While we do not rule out a
contributory role for CHI3L1, the present work is centered on the human
homolog most functionally analogous to Chil3, as determined by genomic and
functional criteria. Future studies will prioritize elucidating the mechanisms of
other CLPs, such as CHID1, in atherogenesis.
We have revised the Discussion section to more accurately articulate
conclusions regarding Chil1 and Chid1, and have added a discussion of the
limitations of the current analysis (Lines 580-592). Future studies will
systematically explore the role of other cholesterol lipoprotein binding proteins,
including CHID1, in atherosclerosis development.

This would require a far more extensive description. Also here the x-axis

acute and chronic infections, malignant tumors, and liver or kidney
insufficiency), while the atherosclerosis group comprised patients diagnosed by

10) Extended Fig 2d. What do the authors mean with a proliferative cell?
Answer: In our manuscript, the term "proliferative cell" refers to a
transcriptional state of cells that are actively progressing through the cell cycle,
rather than a distinct cellular lineage. This definition is robustly supported by
our scRNA-seq data. The cluster we annotated as "proliferative" is
characterized by a strong and coordinated expression of genes that are
hallmark indicators of active cell division. The gene list provided by you is
exemplary of this signature, including:
 Core mitotic regulators: Mki67 (a universal marker for proliferation),
Top2a, Nusap1, Aspm, Ube2c, and Pttg1.
 Histone genes: Hist1h1b/c/d/e, Hist1h4c (synthesized during DNA
replication in S phase).
 Chromatin assembly and structural proteins: Hmgb1/2, Hmgn2, H2afv, Tuba1b, Tubb (critical for chromosome segregation and cytokinesis in M
phase).
The enrichment of this gene set is a well-established signature for cells in the
G2 and M phases of the cell cycle. We observed this proliferative cluster in
spatial proximity to T cell-rich regions in human atherosclerotic plaques, which
may suggest localized cell division activity within the plaque microenvironment.

scale, it corresponds to a substantial and statistically significant increase in the
raw, untransformed data. The use of a non-zero y-axis intercept was solely
intended to visualize this statistically significant log-transformed difference
more clearly, not to overstate its biological importance.

dataset and the human plasma data addressed in Question #6. The human

differentiated into macrophages employing PMA.
Answer: We agree with you that increasing the number of biological replicates
strengthens statistical confidence. In direct response to this point, we have
repeated the key experiments and increased the sample size from n=3 to n=4-
6 (Fig. 31 in this letter, Extended Data Fig. g-j in the revised manuscript). It
should be particularly noted that in the THP-1 cell line experiment (Fig. 31c in
this letter), an average value was obtained after each technical repeat well.
The current data was repeated three times, and the average values of the six
times were analyzed in combination with the results of the previous three times.
Fig. 31. The CLP level in macrophages.
We appreciate your valid point about the activated nature of PMA-differentiated
THP-1 macrophages. In this specific part of our study, the experimental goal
was not to fully model primary human macrophage biology, but rather to
perform a controlled, initial functional screening to identify the human CLPs that
most closely mirrors the polarization behavior of mouse Chil3. While PMA
induces a degree of activation, these cells are widely recognized as resembling
M0 macrophages, with low expression of canonical M1 or M2 markers
compared with fully polarized CAMs/M1 or AAM/M2 cells65-67, making them a
standard model for studying macrophage polarization. Consistent with this, our
data show that CHI3L2, but not CHI3L1, induces marker expression patterns
that faithfully recapitulate the polarization behavior observed for mouse Chil3,
confirming the validity of this screening system12-14. In addition, PBMCs also
need to differentiate their monocytes into macrophages in vitro using PMA, and
then further polarize them into different phenotypes. Of course, we agree with
you and have also noted the potential impact of PMA stimulation, but we believe
it does not affect our conclusion in this study.
13) Fig 4a. More examples on co-localization would need to be shown. The
examples in Fig 4b on co-localization are too unclear to draw conclusions.
Answer: Thanks. Specifically, we have now collected a substantial number of
additional images confirming the co-localization of CLPs with macrophages in
mouse atherosclerotic plaques (n=4 biological replicates) (Fig. 32a, b in this
letter, Fig. 4a and Extended Data Fig. 4a in the revised manuscript). For human
atherosclerotic tissue samples, we have provided enlarged views of the
immunofluorescence staining for clearer visualization. White arrows have been
added to explicitly indicate the co-localization of CHI3L2 with CD68-positive
macrophages (Fig. 32c in this letter, Fig. 4b and Extended Data Fig. 4b in the
revised manuscript).
Fig. 32. Colocalization of CLPs and macrophages.
14) Fig 4b. What is meant by APS and FPS? Again, there is an unclarity here.
This makes it hard to read and properly review this manuscript.
Answer: The abbreviations APS (atheromatous plaque stage) and FPS
(fibrous plaque stage) were defined when initially introduced in the manuscript
(Lines 170-171) and have been maintained consistently thereafter.
15) Fig 4h. The chlodronate experiment is usually performed as a way to study
monocyte infiltration into atherosclerotic plaques. The transferred monocytes
are labeled with beads, so that homing of monocytes to plaques can be studied.
Such an experiment is actually never performed with bone marrow derived
macrophages. If performed in this way, macrophages need to be labeled so
their fate can be studied better. It is unclear what the authors have done in Fig
4h-k. It seems rather to me that they have performed a bone marrow
transplantation without performing the irradiation first. If the authors claim that
the phenotype is macrophage-driven, they will need to create a macrophage-
specific knockout. That is only the proper way that is widely accepted in the
field.
Answer: In this manuscript, we employed the macrophage adoptive
transferring experiment primarily to investigate the role of macrophage-derived
CLPs in atherosclerosis. Specifically, 8-week-old male recipient ApoE-/-.Chil3∆
CD45.1 mice were fed a WD for 13 weeks. At the start of weeks 12 and 13, the
recipient mice were intraperitoneally injected with clodronate liposomes to
deplete macrophages. Macrophage-scavenging agents, such as clodronate
liposomes (Liposoma BV), are a class of compounds specifically designed to
deplete macrophages. Clodronate liposomes are well-established, convenient,
and cost-effective tools for macrophage depletion across various tissues,
including the liver, spleen, lungs, and blood. After two days of clodronate
liposome treatment, macrophage depletion is nearly complete. Following this,
BMDMs from donor CD45.2 (ApoE-/-, ApoE-/-.Chil3∆ and ApoE-
/-.Chil3∆.hCHI3L2tg) mice were transferred into the recipient mice via tail vein
injection to assess the impact of macrophage CLPs on atherosclerosis. The
successful accumulation of transferred CD45.2 macrophages in the aorta was
detected by flow cytometry shown in Extended data Fig. 4f in the revised
manuscript. This experimental technique has been validated in various disease
models, including atherosclerosis, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease and
inflammatory lung diseases12,68,69.
We fully agree with your proposal to establish a macrophage-specific
knockout model. Given the specific expression of Chil3 in macrophages, we
believe our animal model strategy effectively demonstrates the impact of
macrophage-derived Chil3 on atherosclerosis. In contrast, CHI3L2 is widely
expressed; therefore, to specifically investigate the role of myeloid-derived
CHI3L2 in atherosclerosis progression, we additionally generated mice with
macrophage specific knock in CHI3L2 (M-CHI3L2ki/wt). We established another
mouse model by injecting an adeno-associated virus-8 carrying a mutant
PCSK9 gene (AAV8-PCSK9) into M-CHI3L2ki/wt and control mice
(M-CHI3L2wt/wt). These AAV8-PCSK9 mice were fed a WD for three months,
after which plaque burden was assessed (Fig. 33a in this letter). Compared
to M-CHI3L2wt/wt controls, M-CHI3L2ki/wt mice exhibited more extensive lesions
throughout the entire aorta and aortic root, along with increased plaque burden
and greater plaque instability (Fig. 33b, c in this letter). These new results are
included in the Fig. 4f-h in the revised manuscript.
Fig. 33. Effects of macrophage-specific knock-in CHI3L2 on
atherosclerosis.
16) Extended Fig. 4f. The flow cytometry plots are insufficient in showing that
the transfer with macrophages actually led to accumulation of considerable
amount of macrophages in the aorta. The method needs to be established first.
Answer: In our study, CD45.1 recipient mice were intravenously injected with
CD45.2 BMDMs following macrophage depletion. The presence of CD45.2+
cells in both circulation and aortic tissue, as detected by flow cytometry,
provides direct evidence for the successful recruitment and accumulation of
transferred macrophages. The control group (without CD45.2+ BMDM injection)
showed no detectable CD45.2+ cells, confirming the specificity of our detection.
Therefore, the presence of CD45.2+ cells in recipient mice unequivocally
demonstrates the successful accumulation of transferred macrophages in the
aorta. This methodology has been previously validated and widely applied in
atherosclerosis research, as referenced in our manuscript68.This result showed
in Extended data Fig. 4h of the revised manuscript. In addition, as mentioned
in question 15, we have incorporated the CLP macrophage-specific knock-in
experiment to further substantiate the significant role of macrophages in CLP-
regulated atherosclerosis.
17) Extended Fig 5a-c. These calculated interactions actually do not tell us that
much. What is exactly happening here and what is the biological nature of these
interactions.
Answer: Thanks for pointing it out, we basically agree. Our primary aim was to
investigate how CLPs influence macrophages and to identify their key cellular
targets within the atherosclerotic aortic environment. Because CLPs are
predominantly expressed and secreted by macrophages, we explored the
potential for auto/paracrine signaling. The major novel finding of this study is
that CLPs target the macrophage LDL receptor CD36, exerting glycosidase
activity to modify CD36 N-linked glycans, regulate CD36-mediated lipid
endocytosis, and secondarily influence the mTOR-PPARγ-ABCG1 lipid efflux
pathway. We agree that while the CellChat interaction data are informative, they
do not yet provide the mechanistic depth expected at this stage. Accordingly,
we have removed the corresponding interaction diagrams and signaling
strength calculations from the manuscript to better align with the article’s scope
and focus.
18) Extended Fig 5d. If the authors really want to draw a conclusion on
macrophages, they need to perform laser capture microscopy on
atherosclerotic plaques, or single cell RNASeq, but they cannot do this by
performing whole RNA extraction on the aorta.
Answer: We thank you for this comment and wish to clarify that the data in
Extended Data Fig. 5d (Fig. 8f in the revised manuscript) were obtained from
primary macrophages treated with ox-LDL in vitro, not from bulk RNA
sequencing of aortic tissue. Therefore, the conclusions drawn from this figure
specifically reflect the inflammatory response of macrophages under controlled
conditions. We have revised the figure legend and main text to clearly indicate
the experimental source to prevent any potential misunderstanding.
Furthermore, our scRNA-seq analysis of aortic macrophages from
atherosclerotic mice confirmed that CLP expression enhances the transcription
of key inflammatory factors, including Il1b, Il6, and Tnf (Fig. 34 in this letter).
Fig. 34. The inflammatory factors levels.
19) Extended Fig 5e. When were these macrophages isolated? It is impossible
to directly isolate BMDMs; then these cells would be bone marrow monocytes.
This would need to be clarified. How was the experiment performed?
Answer: The two primary murine macrophage types used in this study, namely
peritoneal macrophages (PMφ) and BMDMs, are well-established models
widely employed in atherosclerosis-related in vitro research3,70,71. Both cell
types were isolated from 6- to 8-week-old genetically modified mice maintained
on a standard chow diet, rather than a Western diet. To evaluate the role of
CLPs in macrophage lipid accumulation, we stimulated these primary
macrophages with ox-LDL to induce foam cell formation in vitro.
PMφ were obtained following intraperitoneal injection of 2 mL 3% thioglycolate
broth. Three days later, mice were euthanized, and peritoneal cells were
harvested via lavage with 5 mL ice-cold PBS/EDTA and centrifuged at
1,200 rpm for 10 min at 4 °C. Cells were then lysed with ACK buffer, centrifuged
again, and cultured in DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS and 1% PS. After
6 h, non-adherent cells were removed, and fresh DMEM was added for
subsequent experiments.
BMDMs were generated by flushing the bone marrow cavities of femurs and
tibias under aseptic conditions, filtering the cell suspension through a 40 μm
strainer, centrifuging at 1,200 rpm for 10 min, lysing with ACK buffer, and
washing with PBS. Cells were then seeded at 2 ×106 cells/mL in DMEM
containing 10% FBS and macrophage colony-stimulating factors (M-CSF, 10
ng/mL) for 7 days. As detailed in the Methods section (Lines 866-882), BMDMs
were generated by differentiating bone marrow cells in vitro for 7 days in
medium containing M-CSF. The resulting adherent cells are widely recognized
and referred to as BMDMs in the literature3,70,71.
20) Extended Fig 5f-j. Same questions-how were these experiments performed?
This needs to be stated in the Figure legends or better described in the main
text. If the authors claim more ox-LDL uptake, ideally, they perform mass-spec
on their macrophages to show that free cholesterol and cholesteryl esters are
increased. This is the only definitive measure. These MFI measurements tell us
very little, and again, in extended Fig 5j, differences are minor for BMDMs. I do
not understand the significant p-values. The authors are making too much of
these data.
Answer: Macrophages were pretreated with varying concentrations of
recombinant Chil3 protein for 4 h at 37 °C, followed by incubation with Dil-ox-
LDL (30 μg/mL) for 2 h. Cells were then detached with 0.25% trypsin-EDTA,
pelleted by centrifugation at 1000 × g for 5 min, washed three times with ice-
cold PBS, and resuspended for flow cytometry analysis (full details in Methods,
Lines 904-909).
While MS is the gold standard for quantifying intracellular cholesterol, the Dil-
ox-LDL uptake assay measures a distinct but equally important process:
receptor-mediated lipoprotein internalization. The mean fluorescence intensity
(MFI) reflects the total ox-LDL actively internalized and localized inside the cell,
providing a direct functional readout of scavenger receptor activity72,73. An
increase in Dil-MFI indicates enhanced CD36-dependent endocytosis, the
upstream event driving lipid accumulation detected by mass spectrometry.
Following your suggestion, we also quantified cellular lipids by MS (Fig. 35 in
this letter). These results confirm that CLPs significantly elevate intracellular
free cholesterol and cholesteryl esters in macrophages, consistent with
increased lipid uptake. These data are included in the ABCG1-related
mechanism section (Fig. 8c in the revised manuscript), which addresses the
metabolic consequences of lipid loading, whereas the current section focuses
on the initial effects of CLPs on lipid uptake.
Fig. 35. Intracellular lipid levels using MS.
Finally, we clarify the interpretation of our data. Although the MFI differences in
BMDMs were more modest than those in PMφ, this variation may reflect factors
such as the batch of recombinant Chil3 protein, macrophage lineage, or
variations in the Dil-ox-LDL preparation used. Nevertheless, the statistical
significance in BMDMs arises from the low variability and high consistency
within each group, where even small shifts in mean values can yield robust p-
values, reflecting reproducible biological effects.
Importantly, the enhancing effect of recombinant Chil3 on ox-LDL uptake was
consistently observed across two independent primary macrophage types.
While the response was strong and highly significant in PMφ, the same
directional trend, milder but statistically significant, was reproducibly detected
in BMDMs. This consistency supports the conclusion that Chil3 promotes lipid
uptake, evidenced by both a pronounced effect in peritoneal macrophages and
a reproducible, statistically supported effect in BMDMs.
21) Fig 6i-k. Were these intracellular staining? Ideally the authors would
complement these data with mass spec measurements of free cholesterol and
cholesteryl esters.
Answer: We thank your comment, which allows us to clarify the principles of
the Dil-ox-LDL flow cytometry assay. This method does not represent a
conventional intracellular staining protocol, but rather provides a quantitative
assessment of receptor-mediated internalization. Dil, a lipophilic fluorescent
dye, is covalently incorporated into the lipid core of ox-LDL. When incubated
with macrophages at 37°C, Dil-ox-LDL binds scavenger receptors such as
CD36 and is subsequently internalized via receptor-mediated endocytosis. The
fluorescence detected by flow cytometry originates from internalized particles
within endosomal/lysosomal compartments, as membrane-bound ox-LDL is
removed by stringent washing. Thus, MFI directly reflects scavenger receptor
activity by indicating the extent of ox-LDL uptake3.
Regarding CD36, literature shows that it contains a large, glycosylated
extracellular domain that harbors the ligand-binding site74,75. CD36 also exists
in a soluble form corresponding to its extracellular domain (ECD), generated
through proteolytic cleavage76. In our rescue experiments, we used a
recombinant CD36 protein encoded by the mouse or human ECD sequence
(Gly30–Lys439) with an N-terminal signal peptide and a C-terminal His tag.
Therefore, rCD36Gly30-Lys439 and rCD36ECD refer to the same protein.
Our findings suggest that Chil3 and CHI3L2 bind to CD36 and promote its
endocytosis. To further test this, we performed a competition assay using
exogenous recombinant CD36 (rCD36ECD). Chil3 or CHI3L2 were pre-
incubated with species-matched rCD36ECD, allowing the formation of CLP–
CD36 complexes and reducing the number of free CLPs. This mixture was then
applied to macrophages, followed by Dil-ox-LDL uptake analysis. Notably, the
complex solution markedly reduced lipid uptake compared with recombinant
CLPs alone, supporting our conclusion that Chil3 and CHI3L2 compete for
CD36 binding and modulate lipid uptake. Details are provided in the revised
manuscript (Lines 385-401).
We also agree that MS quantification of intracellular free cholesterol and
cholesteryl esters would be an excellent way to evaluate downstream lipid
accumulation and foam cell formation. These approaches address distinct but
complementary questions: our current data examine the “input” step (uptake),
whereas your suggestion examines the “storage” step (accumulation). While
our results clearly show that CLPs enhance lipid uptake, assessing their impact
on subsequent lipid storage is an important direction for future work. We
appreciate this valuable suggestion.
22) Text line 474. The authors imply that Mylip would be involved in the
cholesterol efflux pathway while it in fact induces the degradation of the Ldl
receptor.
Answer: We thank you for the insightful comment and for pointing out our
misinterpretation of MYLIP function. MYLIP (IDOL) primarily regulates
cholesterol uptake by promoting LDL receptor ubiquitination and degradation,
rather than directly affecting ABCA1/ABCG1-mediated cholesterol efflux. We
apologize for this oversight and have accordingly reclassified Mylip under
cholesterol influx (Fig. 36 in this letter, Extended Data Fig. 8a in the revised
manuscript).
Fig. 36. Heatmap of cholesterol-related genes.
23) Fig 8. It is of interest that mainly Abcg1 is affected in Chil3 deficiency. How
do the authors explain that this particular transporter is affected and not Abca1?
What would the mechanism be underlying this finding?
Answer: When examining cholesterol-metabolism-related proteins in BMDMs
of different genotypes (ApoE-/-, ApoE-/-.Chil3∆ and ApoE-/-.Chil3∆.hCHI3L2tg)
under ox-LDL stimulation, we found that among the major cholesterol efflux
receptors, only ABCG1 was markedly upregulated in CLP-deficient cells,
whereas ABCA1 remained unchanged (Fig. 37a in this letter). This pattern
suggests that CLPs primarily influence cholesterol handling through the
ABCG1-mediated efflux pathway.
We further observed that CLP deficiency significantly increased PPARγ
expression in BMDMs under ox-LDL stimulation. While the classical view
attributes PPARγ-mediated cholesterol efflux mainly to the LXRα-ABCA1 axis42,
growing evidence indicates that PPARγ also suppresses foam-cell formation
through ABCA1-independent mechanisms43. Although both ABCG1 and
ABCA1 are LXRα target genes, their transcriptional sensitivities and responses
to lipid environments differ substantially. Notably, prior studies have shown that
PPARγ agonists can reduce foam cell formation without altering LXRα or
ABCA1 expression43. These findings offer a mechanistic explanation for both
LXR-independent and LXR-dependent regulation of macrophage foam cell
formation44.
In our RT-qPCR analysis, we observed a modest increase in ABCA1 mRNA
levels in ApoE-/- or ApoE-/-.Chil3∆ BMDMs compared with their respective
untreated controls. However, Western blotting showed no corresponding
change in ABCA1 protein expression after ox-LDL stimulation across all
genotypes (Fig. 37a in this letter, Extended data Fig. 8b in the revised
manuscript). This strongly suggests that in the ox-LDL-stimulated foam cell
model, ABCA1 protein may undergo complex post-translational regulation.
For instance, its ubiquitination degradation pathway could be activated, or it might
be degraded within lysosomes, leading to accelerated protein turnover and
preventing net protein accumulation.
Moreover, LXRα expression remained unchanged across all genetically
modified BMDMs (Fig. 37b in this letter), indicating that the classical LXRα–
ABCA1 transcriptional axis was not effectively activated. Several mechanisms
may account for this heterogeneity in LXRα and ABCA1 regulation. First, foam
cells may accumulate high levels of ox-LDL, whose cytotoxic effects can
suppress LXRα expression or promoter activity, thereby limiting Abca1 protein
induction45. Alternatively, foam cell-like macrophages may become more
phagocytic, consistent with known dendritic cell characteristics. This could lead
to phagocytosis of LXRα agonists (ligands)45. These results have been included
in the revised manuscript as Fig. 8a, Extended Data Fig. 8d and Discussion
section (Lines 646-658).
Fig. 37. The expression of cholesterol-related molecules.
24) Related to this, Abcg1 deficiency does not affect atherosclerotic lesion area
or decreases it. This does not align with the findings of the authors. Please
explain.
Answer: We acknowledge that recent studies have reported seemingly
conflicting roles of macrophage ABCG1 in murine atherosclerosis77,78. However,
these investigations assessed ABCG1 deletion as an isolated variable. In
contrast, our model reflects a more integrated pathophysiological context:
ABCG1 downregulation is not an initiating event in atherogenesis but a
downstream consequence of a potent CLP-induced signaling cascade.
In our system, CLPs enhance CD36-dependent lipid uptake, driving substantial
ox-LDL internalization and subsequent mTOR activation. This axis promotes a
pro-inflammatory macrophage state, suppresses PPARγ, and ultimately
reduces ABCG1 expression. Thus, decreased ABCG1 is one element of a
broader pro-atherogenic program.
In conventional Abcg1-/- models, lifelong transporter deficiency triggers
systemic and cellular compensation, including increased ABCA1 and ApoA1
expression, which can mitigate lipid accumulation and lesion progression under
certain dietary conditions77. The resulting phenotype therefore reflects both the
primary mutation and long-term adaptive remodeling.
By contrast, in our setting, ABCG1 downregulation occurs in macrophages
simultaneously subjected to overwhelming CD36-driven lipid influx. Under
these conditions, residual or compensatory efflux pathways are rapidly
saturated, and the loss of ABCG1 synergizes with excessive lipid uptake to
exacerbate lipid retention, inflammation, and plaque progression.
25) How would lipid deposition activate mTOR?
Answer: Nutrients derived from lysosomal degradation such as sugars, lipids,
and amino acids are well-established activators of mTOR, particularly the
mTORC1 complex50-52. In our study, we propose that exogenous lipids,
especially ox-LDL, serve as the primary trigger for mTOR activation in
macrophages. After internalization, ox-LDL is delivered to lysosomes, where
cholesterol esters are hydrolyzed by lysosomal acid lipase (LAL), releasing free
cholesterol and fatty acids46. These liberated lipids, particularly cholesterol, are
sensed within the lysosomal lumen through the established NPC1/NPC2
transport system and the v-ATPase-Ragulator-Rag GTPase axis47-49. Lipid
sensing induces conformational changes in Rag GTPases that recruit mTORC1
to the lysosomal membrane, enabling full activation in the presence of
additional growth signals such as Akt pathway activity79.
Our data functionally validate this lysosome-dependent nutrient-sensing model.
As shown in the newly added figure (Fig. 38 in this letter), ox-LDL-induced
mTOR activation was completely abolished by bafilomycin A1 (Baf-A1), which
blocks lysosomal acidification and function. Any mTOR activation arising from
non-lysosomal inputs, such as signaling through surface receptors or upstream
kinases, would remain intact under Baf-A1 treatment. Thus, our results strongly
support the conclusion that ox-LDL activates mTOR in macrophages through
the canonical lysosomal nutrient-sensing machinery. The result has been
included in the revised manuscript as Extended Data Fig. 8e and are discussed
in the Discussion section (Lines 675-687).
Fig. 38. The effect of Baf-A1 on mTOR.
26) Line 557 – the authors are discussing ‘inflammatory foamy macrophages’.
But the foamy macrophages are generally considered to be anti-inflammatory.
Answer: Sorry. We have re-analyzed our scRNA-seq data (Fig. 39 in this
letter). We identified seven macrophage subpopulations in atherosclerotic
aortas: Ly6C2+ monocyte-like, resident, MHC-II, inflammatory, foamy, VSMC-
like, and fibrochondrocyte (FC)-like macrophages. Chil3 was specifically
enriched in Ly6C2+ monocyte-like macrophages in ApoE-/- mice, whereas
CHI3L2 was mainly expressed in foam cells, VSMC-like macrophages, and FC-
like macrophages in ApoE-/-.Chil3∆.hCHI3L2tg mice. Functionally, Chil3
increased inflammatory macrophages and reduced resident macrophages,
while CHI3L2 expanded foam cell/FC-like clusters at the expense of resident
and MHC-II macrophages (Fig. 39 in this letter). These differences are
consistent with the fact that Chil3 and CHI3L2 are not direct orthologs and
exhibit subtype-specific patterns and consequences. The new results have
been included in the revised manuscript as Fig. 3d-f and Extended Data Fig.
3b.
Fig. 39. The scRNA-seq data.
Minor:
1) Keywords: atherosclerogenesis (also in lines 101 and 110). This is not a
usual word. It is atherosclerosis or atherogenesis.
Answer: Thanks. We have corrected this throughout the manuscript. The term
“atherosclerogenesis” has been replaced with “atherogenesis” in all relevant
sections (including lines 101 and 110) to accurately describe plaque formation.
2) Introduction: line 82 – it probably needs to state: various transformations,
such as those into…
Answer: Thanks. We have changed it to “such as those into”.
3) Also in lines 83-84 it is implied that the switch to other phenotypes accounts
for SMCs taking up lipid. This is simply not true. Lipid uptake by SMCs accounts
for their differentiation into macrophages for example. Please adjust the text
accordingly.
Answer: Thanks. We have changed it to “These phenotypic transitions, which
can be initiated by lipid uptake, enable VSMCs to contribute significantly to
plaque development through enhanced lipid accumulation and calcification”.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
I have carefully reviewed the revised manuscript and the authors’ point-by-point responses. The revisions have adequately
addressed all previously raised concerns. I have no further comments.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The authors have made a huge work in order to address all the Reviewer’s comments. As a whole, the numerous new data
and explanation strengthen the main message of this manuscript. Few last points must however be clarified.
1. As suggested by the Reviewer, the authors performed a lipidomic analysis that clearly helps to decipher the underlying
mechanisms through which Chil3 modulates lipid metabolism in macrophages. However, non-targeted lipidomic profiling
must be detailed in the Methods section. In addition it is not clear how were expressed the lipidomic data in Fig. 8b-c.
Mol of lipids ? % of total lipids ?
2. Importantly, the following sentence in line 499 must be modified : “The results revealed the loss of CLPs reduced neutral
lipids (Cholesterol (Chol), cholesteryl esters (CE), saturated fatty acids (SFA)) which was ……..”. Only cholesterol esters
(CE) are neutral lipids whereas cholesterol (total cholesterol I guess) is a combination of CE and free cholesterol which is a
hydrophilic lipid (not a neutral lipid). Moreover, SFA are carried out by both neutral lipids such as triglycerides and CE and
amphiphilic lipids such as phospholipids and sphingolipids (not neutral lipids).
3. Figure 2a. How do the authors explain that LDL-C was reduced but not total cholesterol in Chil3 deficiency mice upon
western diet. In addition, such a reduction of total cholesterol was not compensated by an increased HDL-C.
4. Extended Figure 2b. This new Figure is not confusing. The Y-axis is labelled as “Change relative to positive control (%)”.
What is the positive control here ? Moreover, why CHI3L2 protein was not quantified before the initial injection ?
5. Methods section, line 913. This sentence must be corrected. It is written that cells were “treated with serum-free medium
containing HDL (ApoB-depleted serum)”. Is it “serum-free medium” which is depleted in all lipoproteins including HDL or
“ApoB-depleted serum” which is only depleted in ApoB-containing lipoproteins but not HDL?
I guess that it is the second
proposition.
6. The authors propose that the unexpected downregulation of Ldlr and Hmgcr in Chil3 deficient mice while intracellular
cholesterol content was reduced could be explained by the increased expression of Mylip (Extended Data Fig. 8a). Was this
increased Mylip expression also observed in peritoneal macrophages in Extended Data Fig. 8b ?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This manuscript has improved, but still several points remain.
Major:
1) My first point referred to how LDL-c was measured. The authors are not providing any clarity here. They basically state
that they used a Beckman AU5431 analyzer. This analyzer is not used exclusively for cholesterol measurements so
basically the authors have not provided a clear response to my comment. Which assay did the authors carry out exactly?
Also, the authors cannot simply acknowledge my point that they have measured other apoB containing lipoproteins than
LDL-C and still call this LDL-C. That is inaccurate. So, please provide an accurate response to my question as to how LDL-
C is measured and which other lipoproteins are measured concomitantly.
2) I do not agree with the response given to my question 12. PMA definitely activates monocytes/macrophages. PBMCs
require M-CSF to be differentiated in macrophages. The authors can simply acknowledge the caveat of the THP-1
macrophages here.
3) My problem with the response to point 16 (extended Fig 4f) is that macrophages usually do not circulate in blood.
Monocytes circulate in blood and differentiate into macrophages upon recruitment into tissues. I also do not agree with the
authors that the injection of BMDMs into blood is an established way to study the role of macrophages in atherosclerosis.
Since the authors have now included the myeloid specific knockout, the manuscript would be improved if the experiment on
the in vivo transfer of BMDMs would be omitted.
4) In response to point 21, the issue is that DiI is in the phospholipid component of oxLDL while the authors claim effects on
cholesterol (the core of the oxLDL) particle. Again, these data would be strengthened by intracellular cholesterol
measurements.
5) The response to my question 23 is just merely speculation. The discovery of the role of ABCG1 in cholesterol efflux was
after reference 43 was published. It would also suffice to state that the authors cannot really explain this discrepancy. It is
also simply not the case that ‘Although both ABCG1 and ABCA1 are LXRα target genes, their transcriptional sensitivities
and responses to lipid environments differ substantially.’ This statement should not be included in the manuscript. The
authors are also making too much of a difference between data on ABCA1 at the mRNA level and assessed via Western
blot. It is perfectly possible that a slight increase in ABCA1 mRNA does not translate into differences in ABCA1 at the
protein level. Please omit any statements addressing this discrepancy from the manuscript. Also the new text in the discussion in
lines 651-674 is highly speculative and needs to be shortened considerably so that all speculations are removed here and
only the data that have been obtained are discussed briefly.
6) Response to point 24. Again here, this response is not really satisfactory since there is no experimental evidence to
support it. The authors can also simply state that they cannot really explain this and recognize the caveat.

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Polymorphisms of mouse chitinase-like protein 3 (Chil3), a member of the mammalian chitinase-like protein (CLP) family, have been demonstrated to be associated with inflammatory diseases by regulating lipid metabolism. However, the specific immunomodulatory impacts of CLPs, mainly mouse CHIL3 and its human functional homologue chitinase-3-like 2 (CHI3L2), on macrophage cholesterol metabolism and atherosclerosis have remained unclear. Here, we find CLPs (CHIL3 and CHI3L2) accelerate atherogenesis in a macrophage-dependent manner. Mechanistically, we identify an autocrine mechanism through which CLPs regulate cholesterol metabolism in macrophages. Macrophage-secreted CLPs exacerbate lipid uptake by binding to CD36. CLPs exhibit glycosidase activity, targeting and hydrolyzing N-glycosylated glycans on CD36, predominantly at sites N220 and N321, thereby enhancing lipid uptake. Increased lipid influx activates mTOR in macrophages, driving their transition to a pro-inflammatory phenotype while simultaneously suppressing peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARγ) expression and thus impairing ABCG1-mediated cholesterol efflux. Single-cell sequencing reveals that CLPs increase atherosclerotic foamy macrophages, favoring vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMC) transformation into foam and osteoblast-like cells. Additionally, neutralizing antibodies targeting CHI3L2 prevent and treat atherosclerosis. These findings highlight the potential of CLPs as targets for disease diagnosis and therapy.

## Introduction

Identification of key genes regulating metabolic diseases offers valuable insights into disease pathogenesis. In our previous study, we positionally cloned Chil3, encoding chitinase-like protein 3 (CHIL3/Ym1), as a susceptibility gene for inflammatory diseases through its modulation of macrophage lipid metabolism and alternative activation1. CHIL3 belongs to a family of chitinase-like proteins (CLPs), which lack chitinase activity due to mutations in putative enzyme sites2. Mammals possess several identified CLPs, including chitinase-3-like 1 (CHI3L1), CHI3L2, CHIL3, CHIL4, chitinase domain containing 1 (CHID1) and oviductal glycoprotein 1 (OVGP1)3. Notably, CHI3L2 is exclusive to humans and absent in rodents, whereas CHIL3 and CHIL4 are uniquely found in rodents4. Macrophages represent a significant source of both mouse and human CLPs. CHIL3 and CHI3L2 have emerged as markers of alternatively activated macrophages (AAMs)1,5, whereas CHI3L1 is prominently induced in classically activated macrophages (CAMs)6. CLPs, which contain a conserved glycosyl hydrolase family 18 (GH18) domain, participate in biological processes that contribute to chronic inflammatory and metabolic diseases through shared or molecule-specific immunometabolic functions3.

Atherosclerosis is a chronic, lipid-driven vascular inflammatory disease and a pivotal pathological precursor to cardiovascular diseases (CVD), involving the pathophysiological activation of macrophages, vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) and endothelial cells (ECs)7,8. Dysregulation of cholesterol homeostasis in macrophages, mediated by the interplay of oxidized low-density lipoprotein (ox-LDL) uptake through scavenger receptors and cholesterol efflux, leads to macrophage dysfunction9,10. Furthermore, VSMCs are the main cellular component of advanced atherosclerotic aortas and are highly plastic cells that can undergo various phenotypic transformations, such as those into mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs), macrophage-like and osteochondrocyte-like cells11. These phenotypic transitions, which can be initiated by lipid uptake, enable VSMCs to contribute significantly to plaque development through enhanced lipid accumulation and calcification11. Identifying the molecular mechanisms controlling foam cell formation and retention within plaques holds promise for discovering potential clinical diagnostic markers and therapeutic targets for atherosclerosis. However, CLPs lacking chitinase activity have been poorly studied in atherosclerosis. Clinical studies have demonstrated a positive correlation between elevated serum CHI3L1/CHI3L2 levels and coronary artery disease development, plasma triglyceride (TG), and total cholesterol (TC) levels12-16. Only a few experimental studies have reported that CHI3L1 is associated with macrophage apoptosis, EC inflammation and activation of VSMCs, thereby exacerbating atherosclerosis17,18. Overall, there remains an absence of experimental evidence linking CLPs to immunometabolic regulation in chronic inflammatory diseases such as atherosclerosis. Our study aims to explore the involvement of CHIL3 and its human functional homologue CLP in the modulation of atherosclerosis.

Herein, we reveal that CLPs, specifically human-specific CHI3L2 and mouse-specific CHIL3, are markedly induced in atherosclerotic macrophages, and in particular alter the phenotypic transition of macrophages and VSMCs, skewing them towards a disease-promoting phenotype. Interventions targeting these CLPs can influence atherogenesis. Mechanistically, CLPs exhibit glycosidase activity, leading to scavenger receptor cluster of differentiation 36 (CD36) deglycosylation, thereby regulating lipid uptake. Additionally, CLPs play a crucial role in modulating cholesterol efflux and the immune-inflammatory state of macrophages. Moreover, the significant efficacy of neutralizing antibodies against CHI3L2 in treating atherosclerosis underscores the potential of CLPs as promising targets for precise diagnostic and therapeutic strategies. Together, these findings highlight the profound impact and intricate mechanisms of CLPs in atherosclerosis.
